title: Glauber dynamics of the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model: a dynamical cavity method
summary: We present a closed theory, exact in the $N\to\infty$ limit, of the equilibrium spin correlations of the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model evolving with Glauber dynamics, above and at the transition temperature $T_c$. The derivation uses a dynamic cavity approach: in the evolution equation for the selected spin the other spins are represented by a fluctuating field. The influence of the selected spin on this field is included at the linear response level; it is given as a sum of the spin's past flips weighted by the correlations of the unperturbed fluctuating field. The self-consistency condition relates the time-dependent correlations of the selected spin and those of the fluctuating field. The theory predicts a $(T-T_c)^{-2}$ divergence of the relaxation time upon approaching the transition and an $At^{-1/2}$ decay of spin correlations at $T_c$. A numerical solution of the theory gives the amplitude, $A=0.964\pm 0.007$. The theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with Glauber dynamics computer simulations.

AI.tldr: A closed, exact (N→∞) dynamic cavity theory for equilibrium spin correlations of the SK spin glass under Glauber dynamics above and at Tc, predicting (T−Tc)^−2 relaxation-time divergence, At^−1/2 decay at Tc with A=0.964±0.007, matching simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing treatments of equilibrium spin correlations in the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model under Glauber dynamics lacked a closed, exact theory above and at the transition. The authors aim to derive such a theory to characterize critical slowing down and correlation decay precisely.
AI.method: Dynamic cavity approach: in the evolution equation for a selected spin, all other spins are replaced by a fluctuating field. The back-reaction of the selected spin on this field is included at linear-response level as a sum of the spin's past flips weighted by correlations of the unperturbed fluctuating field. A self-consistency condition then relates time-dependent correlations of the selected spin to those of the fluctuating field, yielding closed equations exact in the N→∞ limit.
AI.result: The theory predicts a (T−Tc)^−2 divergence of the relaxation time as T→Tc and an At^−1/2 decay of spin correlations at Tc. Numerical solution gives the amplitude A=0.964±0.007. Predictions agree excellently with Glauber dynamics computer simulations.
AI.conclusion: The dynamic cavity theory provides an exact (N→∞) closed description of equilibrium spin correlations in the SK model above and at Tc, correctly capturing critical slowing down and the anomalous t^−1/2 decay, validated by simulation.

title: Optical Ceiling on Polaron Mobility in Disordered Molecular Semiconductors: Lessons from Eumelanin
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure; ancillary Python code reproduces all numerical results
summary: Polaron hopping in disordered molecular semiconductors such as eumelanin is set by energetic disorder $σ$ and reorganization energy $λ$. We show that the reduced polaron absorption band encodes this transport problem. Its value at zero energy fixes the mean hop rate, which bounds the mobility in any dimension. For Gaussian disorder and classical vibrations its centroid is $E_\mathrm{op}=λ+(1-c)σ^2/k_BT$, its variance obeys the Hush relation, and the bound is the Marcus rate at $λ\to E_\mathrm{op}$; a 1D lower bound vanishes at $k_BT^*=(1-c)σ^2/λ$, read from optics.

AI.tldr: The reduced polaron absorption band encodes the polaron transport problem: its zero-energy value fixes the mean hop rate and bounds mobility in any dimension, with closed-form optical expressions for $E_\mathrm{op}$ and $T^*$ for Gaussian disorder.
AI.motivation: In disordered molecular semiconductors like eumelanin, polaron hopping transport is governed by energetic disorder $\sigma$ and reorganization energy $\lambda$, but these parameters are hard to access directly; the authors seek an optical route to the transport problem.
AI.method: Analytical treatment linking the reduced polaron absorption band to hopping kinetics, for Gaussian disorder and classical vibrations, deriving the band centroid, its variance (Hush relation), and mobility bounds across dimensions.
AI.result: The zero-energy absorption value fixes the mean hop rate and bounds mobility in any dimension; the centroid is $E_\mathrm{op}=\lambda+(1-c)\sigma^2/k_BT$; the variance obeys the Hush relation; the bound equals the Marcus rate at $\lambda\to E_\mathrm{op}$; the 1D lower bound vanishes at $k_BT^*=(1-c)\sigma^2/\lambda$, readable from optics.
AI.conclusion: Optical absorption of the reduced polaron band provides a direct, dimension-independent probe of polaron hopping transport, yielding transport bounds and a crossover temperature $T^*$ extractable purely from spectroscopy.

title: Bulk and edge states in Fibonacci-Bose-Hubbard clusters
summary: We study the one- and two-boson energy subspaces of finite open Bose--Hubbard chains with Fibonacci-modulated hopping and zero on-site potential. Their spectra exhibit a hierarchy of bands and gaps, and a critical zero-energy mode for odd lengths, in agreement with prior research. For the singe-excitation subspace we find two families of length-invariant finite-energy states localized at the left cluster boundary. For the two-boson subspace, we report both doublon and separated-pair excitations in the form of Tamm/Shockley states localized near either end. In particular, the right-edge doublon states occur across all Fibonacci generations whereas the left-side states appear every second generation. We check numerically that the second-order perturbation theory accounts well for the structure of the spectrum and the edge states in the doublon subspace in the strong-coupling regime. The results are useful for future explorations of many-body physics beyond numerical tractability, specifically using near-term Josephson quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: Spectral and edge-state analysis of one- and two-boson subspaces in finite open Bose–Hubbard chains with Fibonacci-modulated hopping, revealing length-invariant single-excitation edge states, doublon/separated-pair Tamm–Shockley states, and a generation-dependent pattern of left-edge doublons.
AI.motivation: Prior work established band/gap hierarchies and a critical zero-energy mode in Fibonacci-modulated Bose–Hubbard chains, but the nature of localized edge states in the few-boson subspaces and their dependence on chain length and Fibonacci generation remained unclear.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization of one- and two-boson subspaces of finite open Bose–Hubbard chains with Fibonacci-modulated hopping and zero on-site potential; identification of localized Tamm/Shockley-type states; comparison with second-order perturbation theory in the strong-coupling (doublon) regime.
AI.result: Spectra show a hierarchy of bands and gaps plus a critical zero-energy mode for odd lengths. The single-excitation subspace hosts two families of length-invariant finite-energy states localized at the left cluster boundary. The two-boson subspace supports both doublon and separated-pair Tamm/Shockley states at either end; right-edge doublons occur in all Fibonacci generations while left-side states appear every second generation. Second-order perturbation theory reproduces the doublon spectrum and edge states well in the strong-coupling regime.
AI.conclusion: Fibonacci-modulated open Bose–Hubbard chains host robust, generation-dependent edge and doublon states whose structure is captured perturbatively, making them promising targets for near-term Josephson quantum simulators exploring many-body physics beyond numerical tractability.

title: Quantum banking system for secure cash withdrawal
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Theoretical proposal of a Quantum Teller Machine (QTM) for secure cash withdrawal using quantum-token authentication and NV-center spin qubits
summary: A quantum-secure withdrawal framework is presented by replacing reproducible classical credentials with quantum tokens for authentication. The protocol integrates token generation, authentication, and verification into the existing banking workflow using experimentally motivated quantum control techniques. This mitigates card cloning, credential theft, and counterfeiting.

AI.tldr: A withdrawal protocol replaces reproducible classical credentials with quantum tokens for authentication, integrating token generation, authentication, and verification into existing banking workflows to mitigate card cloning, credential theft, and counterfeiting.
AI.motivation: Classical banking credentials are reproducible, enabling card cloning, credential theft, and counterfeiting. The work aims to provide quantum-secure authentication for withdrawals.
AI.method: A quantum-token-based authentication framework in which reproducible classical credentials are replaced by quantum tokens, with token generation, authentication, and verification integrated into existing banking workflow using experimentally motivated quantum control techniques.
AI.result: The proposed protocol mitigates card cloning, credential theft, and counterfeiting by exploiting the non-reproducibility of quantum tokens for authentication.
AI.conclusion: Quantum tokens offer a practical path to hardening withdrawal authentication against credential-copying attacks while remaining compatible with existing banking workflows.

title: Optimised finite key for satellite up-link entangled quantum key distribution
comment: 16 pages including supplementary material, with 10 figures and 2 tables. Comments welcome
summary: Entanglement-based quantum key distribution from ground to satellite has been proposed as a scalable primitive for global quantum networks and will be demonstrated as part of the imminent QEYSSat mission. Both theoretical studies and experimental emulations have shown that a significant asymptotic key rate can be expected. In this work we investigate this scenario with a more rigorous security analysis taking into account the finite size effects that arise from short block lengths common in satellite transmission. Our findings suggest a slight alteration of the optimal source operation when informed by finite statistics as opposed to the asymptotic regime, notably that the pump power should be slightly lowered. We quantify the annual key rate based on a dynamically optimised source operation for the Heriot-Watt ground station and several satellite parameters. We find an improved annual key rate when accumulating all raw key material before extracting a secure key instead of doing so for each overpass. We ultimately show that QEYSSat will be able to generate a significant secure annual key with both strategies.

AI.tldr: Finite-size security analysis of ground-to-satellite entanglement-based QKD for the QEYSSat mission, optimizing source operation and quantifying annual key rates.
AI.motivation: Entanglement-based ground-to-satellite QKD is proposed as a scalable primitive for global quantum networks and will be demonstrated in the QEYSSat mission. Prior asymptotic studies and emulations predict significant key rates, but satellite transmission implies short block lengths, so finite-size effects must be rigorously accounted for to assess realistic performance.
AI.method: Rigorous security analysis incorporating finite-size effects from short block lengths typical of satellite overpasses. The source operation is dynamically optimized under finite statistics rather than the asymptotic regime, and annual key rates are computed for the Heriot-Watt ground station across several satellite parameter sets, comparing per-overpass key extraction versus accumulating all raw key material before extracting a secure key.
AI.result: Finite-statistics analysis suggests a slight modification of optimal source operation versus the asymptotic case, notably lowering the pump power. Accumulating all raw key material before secure-key extraction yields an improved annual key rate compared to per-overpass extraction. QEYSSat is shown to generate a significant secure annual key with both strategies.
AI.conclusion: Finite-size effects materially refine source optimization for satellite entanglement-based QKD, and key accumulation across overpasses is beneficial; QEYSSat is expected to deliver a significant secure annual key under realistic, finite-statistics operation.

title: Long-range entangled criticality from coherent errors
summary: We find that coherent error can induce a phase transition from the clean surface code phase into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length. To demonstrate this, we establish two general results of independent interest. The first relates topology and quantum information to mixed-state entanglement: we show that when a noise channel acting on a topological code preserves a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information, the noisy state for generic logical input is long-range entangled. The second generalizes the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length to any locally parameterized family, thus encompassing local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. We apply these results to the honeycomb surface code, in which we find an extended long-range entangled critical regime that is a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. As a byproduct of these studies, we relate the conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.

AI.tldr: Coherent errors can drive the clean surface code across a phase transition into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length, supported by two general theorems linking topology, higher-form symmetry, and mixed-state entanglement.
AI.motivation: Understanding how coherent errors affect topological quantum codes is central to error correction, yet the fate of the clean surface-code phase under coherent noise—and the mixed-state entanglement structure that emerges—is not established. The authors aim to characterize the phases accessible under such noise.
AI.method: Two general results are proved: (1) if a noise channel acting on a topological code preserves a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information, the noisy state for generic logical input is long-range entangled; (2) the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length is generalized to any locally parameterized family (local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, thermal states). These are applied to the honeycomb surface code, with conditional mutual information related to conductance in a Majorana network model.
AI.result: Coherent errors induce a transition from the clean surface-code phase to an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length. In the honeycomb surface code this regime is a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. Conditional mutual information is connected to conductance in a Majorana network model.
AI.conclusion: Coherent noise fundamentally reshapes the phase diagram of the surface code, producing an extended critical long-range entangled phase rather than immediate decoherence, with the two general theorems providing broadly applicable tools for mixed-state topological order.

title: Entanglement-Aware Quantum Circuit Optimization through Globally Optimal Partitioning
summary: We introduce a scalable framework for globally optimal quantum-circuit partitioning and entanglement-aware block resynthesis. The partitioning problem is formulated as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits, supporting objectives such as minimizing the number of partitions or a weighted execution cost. The resulting partition selection is exact over the enumerated feasible candidates and their computed costs when the ILP is solved to proven optimality. The selected partitions are resynthesized using an operator-Schmidt rank (OSR) based synthesis technique, which exploits their internal entanglement structure. We compare the end-to-end integer linear programming (ILP)--OSR workflow with BQSKit while identifying their different routing methods, and separately compare local OSR and BQSKit synthesis on matched three- and four-qubit unitaries. On the frozen sample of 772 local unitary targets, OSR produces 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit, and matches or improves the CNOT count in all 617 jointly verified pairs. These results demonstrate that globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis improves circuit quality and extends block-based optimization to problem sizes that are impractical for existing optimization workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an exact ILP-based quantum-circuit partitioning framework with entanglement-aware (operator-Schmidt rank) block resynthesis, showing higher synthesis success and lower CNOT counts than BQSKit on small-unit and end-to-end benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing block-based quantum circuit optimization struggles with global optimality in partition selection and does not exploit the internal entanglement structure of selected blocks, limiting scalability and circuit quality.
AI.method: Formulates partitioning as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits with objectives such as minimizing partition count or weighted execution cost; solving the ILP to proven optimality yields exact selection over enumerated feasible candidates. Selected partitions are resynthesized via operator-Schmidt rank (OSR)-based synthesis exploiting internal entanglement structure. The ILP–OSR workflow is compared end-to-end against BQSKit (with routing-method differences identified), plus a controlled local comparison of OSR vs. BQSKit synthesis on matched 3- and 4-qubit unitaries.
AI.result: On 772 local unitary targets, OSR yields 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit; across all 617 jointly verified pairs OSR matches or improves CNOT count. The ILP–OSR workflow improves circuit quality and extends block-based optimization to problem sizes impractical for existing workflows.
AI.conclusion: Globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis improves circuit quality and scalability of block-based quantum-circuit optimization.

title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks
summary: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a physics-informed neural network (PINN) that learns high-fidelity quantum gates for one- and two-qubit systems by solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, then characterizes the learned controls, tests them under dissipation, and compresses them into compact Chebyshev and square-pulse representations for playback.
AI.motivation: Accurate quantum gate synthesis is essential for quantum computing, but learned control fields must satisfy physical constraints, remain faithful under realistic noise, and be storable/reproducible in compact form. The authors aim for a single PINN framework that achieves very high gate fidelity while also addressing control-resource characterization, robustness to dissipation, and compact playback of the resulting controls.
AI.method: A PINN is trained on the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with smooth, fixed-boundary control fields. The loss combines model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization, and multiple initial conditions. Training uses pairs of mutually unbiased bases; validation uses Haar-random states and average gate fidelity. The study covers Hadamard and controlled-NOT gates under XX, YY, and ZZ interactions, examines dependence on coupling, training configuration, and local fields (including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios), and tests the controls under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping. Learned controls are then compressed via boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions and square-pulse/Strang propagation.
AI.result: Unitary simulations give average gate infidelity of 8.49e-8 for Hadamard and 3.39e-7 to 4.96e-6 for controlled-NOT under XX, YY, and ZZ interactions. Under the Lindblad equation, the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime is theoretically reproduced. Boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of K*=24 coefficients per control, keeping all eleven family-averaged MSEs below 1e-6. Square-pulse and Strang propagation at K=30 preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity 1e-5 at N=128 and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules.
AI.conclusion: The results link multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback, showing that PINN-learned controls can achieve near-unitary fidelity, degrade as predicted under weak dissipation, and be compressed into short Chebyshev and reliable square-pulse forms for faithful reproduction.

title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting
summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.

AI.tldr: A six-qubit gate-based quantum reservoir forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts competitively with ridge regression, and hardware-aware layout selection makes its transfer to the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor consistent.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether small quantum reservoir computing (QRC) models can forecast real data competitively with classical baselines, and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware.
AI.method: A six-qubit Trotterized Ising reservoir was selected and frozen from five candidates using hardware-native interaction graphs, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. Forecasting was done on next-day motor-insurance claim counts over 232 held-out test days, benchmarked against ridge regression and classical recurrent/reservoir baselines. On IBM Kingston, 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds compared hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization-level-1 layouts.
AI.result: Ideal candidates reached RMSEs of 5.66-6.12 claims/day versus 5.36 for ridge; four of five were not significantly different under a 95% block bootstrap and were comparable to classical baselines. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), avoiding severe failures of some random layouts. Most distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift detectable by a short hardware probe on training inputs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without consistent accuracy or transfer gains.
AI.conclusion: Small QRC models can reach competitive accuracy on this real forecasting task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent; longer replay windows are not beneficial.

title: Unital qubit channels are $3$-noisy
summary: The algebraic and environmental characteristics of mixed unitary quantum operations are investigated. It is established that the composition of two uniformly n-mixed unitary channels is itself n-noisy, and this n-noisy property is shown to be an invariant under unitary equivalence. Furthermore, by utilizing majorization and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels, we demonstrate that any unital qubit channel can be physically simulated using a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment. Together, these results advance the classification and physical realization of noisy quantum channels.

AI.tldr: This paper studies algebraic and environmental properties of mixed unitary (noisy) quantum channels, showing composition closure of n-noisy channels, unitary-equivalence invariance of the n-noisy property, and that every unital qubit channel can be simulated with a 3-dimensional maximally mixed environment.
AI.motivation: Mixed unitary quantum operations model noise in realistic channels, but their algebraic closure properties and the minimal environmental dimension needed for physical realization are not fully understood. The authors aim to advance the classification and physical simulation of noisy quantum channels.
AI.method: The analysis combines algebraic characterization of uniformly n-mixed unitary channels with majorization techniques and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels; unitary equivalence is used to exhibit invariance of the n-noisy property.
AI.result: The composition of two uniformly n-mixed unitary channels is shown to be n-noisy, and the n-noisy property is proven invariant under unitary equivalence. Moreover, any unital qubit channel is shown to be physically simulable using a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment.
AI.conclusion: These results extend the classification of mixed unitary channels and establish a minimal-environment simulation for unital qubit channels, contributing to the theory and physical realization of noisy quantum operations.

title: Analog quantum simulation of paraparticle statistics
summary: Bosonic and fermionic quantum statistics describe all known elementary and emergent particles in three dimensions, although many attempts have been made to discover other valid quantum statistical frameworks. One recent formulation proposes "$R$-paraparticles," indistinguishable particles with nonlocal internal degrees of freedom governed by generalized exchange rules [Wang and Hazzard, Nature 637, 314 (2025)]. Here, we emulate a species of paraparticle that exhibits a generalized Pauli exclusion principle using a superconducting qubit lattice. We confirm its unique quantum statistics by measuring a $180^\circ$ phase shift under paraparticle exchange, observing antibunching independent of internal degrees of freedom under two-particle interference at a beamsplitter, and finding a thermal occupation inconsistent with both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics. These results demonstrate that parastatistics are observable on quantum simulation platforms, further motivating their use to explore theorized new phases of matter.

AI.tldr: This work emulates a species of paraparticle with generalized Pauli exclusion on a superconducting qubit lattice, confirming its non-Bose/non-Fermi quantum statistics.
AI.motivation: Bosonic and fermionic statistics describe all known particles in three dimensions, but alternative valid quantum statistical frameworks (parastatistics, e.g., "R-paraparticles") have been recently proposed; the authors aim to realize and observe these exotic statistics on a quantum simulation platform.
AI.method: Emulation of a paraparticle species exhibiting a generalized Pauli exclusion principle using a superconducting qubit lattice. Signatures are probed via exchange-phase measurement, two-particle interference at a beamsplitter, and thermal occupation.
AI.result: (1) A 180° phase shift is measured under paraparticle exchange; (2) antibunching independent of internal degrees of freedom is observed in two-particle beamsplitter interference; (3) the measured thermal occupation is inconsistent with both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics.
AI.conclusion: Parastatistics are observable on quantum simulation platforms, motivating their use to explore theorized new phases of matter.

title: Non-Hermitian effective dynamics from post-selection protocols
summary: Multiple seemingly distinct frameworks are commonly proposed to explain the emergence of effective non-Hermitian dynamics in quantum systems coupled to an environment. Furthermore, it remains contested how to properly calculate expectation values or whether thermal equilibrium states exist in non-Hermitian systems. In this work, we show that Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach can all be understood through the Kraus map formalism, leading to non-Hermitian time evolution if an appropriate post-selection procedure is enforced. After first deriving an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics, we discuss the approximations employed in each approach and the classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be obtained. Within this framework, we physically justify the consistency of the right-right formalism (as opposed to the biorthogonal one) for calculating expectation values. Finally, we demonstrate that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium is not applicable to general non-Hermitian systems. Consequently, stationary states are characterized as non-equilibrium steady states, which should not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the system-environment composite.

AI.tldr: Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach are unified under a Kraus map formalism that yields non-Hermitian dynamics under post-selection; this framework justifies the right-right expectation-value formalism and shows thermodynamic equilibrium does not generally apply, so stationary states are non-equilibrium steady states.
AI.motivation: Multiple distinct frameworks are proposed to explain non-Hermitian dynamics in open quantum systems, and it is contested how to compute expectation values (right-right vs. biorthogonal) or whether thermal equilibrium states exist in non-Hermitian systems. The work aims to unify these frameworks and resolve these conceptual disputes.
AI.method: The authors show that Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach can all be cast within the Kraus map formalism, which produces non-Hermitian time evolution when an appropriate post-selection procedure is enforced. They derive an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics, then analyze the approximations used in each approach and the classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians obtainable.
AI.result: Within the unified framework, the consistency of the right-right formalism (as opposed to the biorthogonal one) for calculating expectation values is physically justified. It is also shown that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium is not applicable to general non-Hermitian systems.
AI.conclusion: Stationary states of general non-Hermitian systems should be characterized as non-equilibrium steady states and should not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the system-environment composite.

title: Pump quantization changes optimal measurements for quantum sensing
summary: Standard analyses of quantum phase sensing often neglect the overhead of generating squeezed-light by treating the pump as an undepleted classical resource. Realistically, the pump is a quantum object that undergoes significant depletion and entangles with the produced squeezed light, raising the question of how the crossover from a classical to a quantum pump limits the quantum advantage in sensing. Contrary to prior analyses, we show that quantum advantage persists despite pump quantization, but depends critically on the nonlinear $(χ^{(2)})$ source dynamics. In particular, we demonstrate that Heisenberg scaling emerges in the regime of strong pump depletion, rather than maximum signal squeezing. At maximum squeezing, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for interferometric sensing of an unknown phase scales as $N^{3/2}$, where $N$ is the pump photon number, surpassing the shot-noise limit but establishing that squeezing itself is insufficient to attain Heisenberg scaling of $N^2$. At maximal pump depletion, where the signal flux is maximized, the QFI scales as $N^2$. In this regime, standard photon counting is suboptimal, while a joint nonlinear measurement of the entire pump-signal system is shown to achieve Heisenberg scaling. Our work shows that pump quantization changes both the optimal operating point and the measurement strategies required to preserve a realistic quantum advantage in phase estimation and, more broadly, many-body quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: Quantum advantage in phase sensing persists even with a fully quantized, depleting pump, but its scaling depends critically on χ⁽²⁾ source dynamics: QFI scales as N^{3/2} at maximum squeezing and as N² (Heisenberg) only at maximal pump depletion, where a joint nonlinear pump–signal measurement is required.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum phase-sensing analyses treat the squeezed-light pump as an undepleted classical resource, ignoring the overhead of squeezing generation. In reality the pump is quantum, depletes significantly, and entangles with the signal, so it is unclear whether and how the classical-to-quantum pump crossover limits the achievable quantum advantage.
AI.method: Analyze phase sensing with a quantized pump in a nonlinear χ⁽²⁾ source, tracking pump depletion and pump–signal entanglement. Compute the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for interferometric estimation of an unknown phase as a function of pump photon number N, comparing regimes of maximum signal squeezing versus maximal pump depletion, and evaluate measurement strategies (photon counting vs. joint nonlinear measurement of the pump–signal system).
AI.result: Contrary to prior analyses, quantum advantage survives pump quantization. At maximum squeezing the QFI scales as N^{3/2}—beating the shot-noise limit but not reaching Heisenberg scaling—showing squeezing alone is insufficient. At maximal pump depletion, where signal flux is maximized, QFI scales as N²; standard photon counting is suboptimal there, whereas a joint nonlinear measurement over the entire pump–signal system attains Heisenberg scaling.
AI.conclusion: Pump quantization shifts both the optimal operating point (strong depletion rather than maximum squeezing) and the required measurement strategy for realistic quantum advantage in phase estimation. These findings extend more broadly to many-body quantum dynamics in driven nonlinear sources.

title: The Impact of Internal Electric Fields on Accurate Diamond Magnetometry
summary: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center spin ensembles are a promising platform for accurate vector magnetometry, as they offer measurements referenced to a spin Hamiltonian in an anisotropic crystal with native vector sensing capabilities. However, charged dopants within the diamond produce random internal electric fields (RIEFs) that shift NV spin-transition frequencies, and their impact on the accuracy of NV magnetometry has not been investigated. Here, we characterize RIEFs' effect on NV spin-transition spectra and propose an analytical fitting function to improve accuracy in their presence. We build a Monte Carlo RIEF model that reproduces the asymmetric lineshapes observed in experimental optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, and use it as a testbed to quantify RIEF-induced errors by simulating ODMR spectra including RIEFs and comparing reconstructed magnetic fields to the known model input. With standard analysis approaches, we observe systematic errors exceeding the g-factor uncertainty in fields below $\sim$ 5 mT, while the proposed fitting function reduces the error by nearly an order of magnitude. Our results demonstrate that RIEFs can play a significant role in the systematic error budget for NV magnetometry, and offer a path towards improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: Charged dopants in diamond generate random internal electric fields (RIEFs) that shift NV spin-transition frequencies and cause systematic errors in NV-ensemble vector magnetometry; a Monte Carlo RIEF model reproducing asymmetric ODMR lineshapes quantifies these errors, and a proposed analytical fitting function reduces them by nearly an order of magnitude.
AI.motivation: NV center spin ensembles are attractive for accurate vector magnetometry because they are referenced to a spin Hamiltonian in an anisotropic crystal with intrinsic vector sensitivity. However, charged dopants in the diamond produce random internal electric fields that shift NV spin-transition frequencies, and the impact of these RIEFs on magnetometry accuracy had not previously been investigated.
AI.method: The authors characterize the effect of RIEFs on NV spin-transition spectra and propose an analytical fitting function tailored to their presence. They construct a Monte Carlo RIEF model that reproduces the asymmetric lineshapes seen in experimental ODMR spectra, and use it as a testbed: they simulate ODMR spectra including RIEFs and compare reconstructed magnetic fields against the known model input to quantify RIEF-induced errors, benchmarking standard analysis against the new fitting function.
AI.result: With standard analysis approaches, systematic errors exceed the g-factor uncertainty for fields below approximately 5 mT, whereas the proposed fitting function reduces the error by nearly an order of magnitude. The Monte Carlo model successfully reproduces the asymmetric ODMR lineshapes observed experimentally.
AI.conclusion: RIEFs can be a significant contributor to the systematic error budget of NV magnetometry, particularly at low fields, and the proposed fitting function offers a practical path toward improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.

title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization
summary: Optimizing continuous-variable functions on qubit-based quantum hardware requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible representation of the objective function. Fixed-grid discretizations provide a direct encoding, but restrict the search to a predefined range and resolution; at the same time, constructing a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous-variable objective can be impractical. Here, we introduce a framework for continuous-variable optimization tailored to qubit-based quantum architectures. The method combines an adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian. We assess the approach on unconstrained and constrained instances of the $n$-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark, and on a proof-of-concept inverse-planning problem in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for cancer treatment. The results show that this framework can produce competitive solutions, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.

AI.tldr: A framework combining adaptive discretization with iterative local mapping of continuous objectives onto effective spin-glass Hamiltonians enables continuous-variable optimization on qubit-based quantum hardware, validated on Gramacy-Lee benchmarks and an IMRT inverse-planning problem.
AI.motivation: Running continuous-variable optimization on qubit-based quantum devices requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible encoding of the objective. Fixed-grid discretizations constrain search to a predefined range and resolution, while building a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous objective is impractical.
AI.method: The proposed framework pairs adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping that projects the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian suitable for qubit solvers, refining the discretization around promising regions as optimization proceeds.
AI.result: Evaluated on unconstrained and constrained instances of the n-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark and on a proof-of-concept IMRT inverse-planning problem, the framework yields competitive solutions.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a flexible, solver-agnostic mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines, avoiding the range and resolution limits of fixed grids and the impracticality of exact Hamiltonian construction.

title: Tight Quasiprobabilistic Entropic Uncertainty Relations for Discrete Quantum Systems
summary: It was conjectured by Wehrl and proven by Lieb that the Shannon differential entropy of the Husimi function of a continuous-variable quantum state is lower bounded by the value it takes on coherent states. This corroborates the intuition, familiar from Heisenberg's uncertainty relations, that coherent states are minimal uncertainty states. The analogous statement for the Wigner function would be that the Wigner differential entropy of states with a positive Wigner function is bounded below by the entropy of pure Gaussian states. This was conjectured a decade ago, but recently disproven. Here, we prove the analogous statement for Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with mutually unbiased bases and for the Gross-Wigner distributions. For these discrete systems, the entropy-minimizing role is played by the pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions. Further, we prove that Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with large nonpositivity have large uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper proves entropy lower bounds for Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with mutually unbiased bases and for Gross-Wigner distributions, showing that pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions minimize the entropy, and that large KD nonpositivity implies large uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Wehrl-Lieb established that the Shannon entropy of the Husimi function is minimized by coherent states, but the analogous conjecture for the Wigner function (entropy minimized by pure Gaussian states among positive-Wigner states) has recently been disproven. This motivates examining whether an analogous entropy-minimization principle holds for other quasiprobability distributions, specifically discrete Kirkwood-Dirac and Gross-Wigner distributions.
AI.method: The authors prove entropy lower bounds for Kirkwood-Dirac distributions constructed from mutually unbiased bases and for Gross-Wigner distributions, identifying the entropy-minimizing states as pure states whose quasiprobability distributions are nonnegative. They additionally establish a quantitative link between KD nonpositivity and uncertainty.
AI.result: For both the KD distributions with mutually unbiased bases and the Gross-Wigner distributions, the Shannon entropy is bounded below, with the minimum attained by pure states having positive quasiprobability distributions. Furthermore, states with large Kirkwood-Dirac nonpositivity are shown to have large uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: An entropy-minimization principle analogous to the Wehrl-Lieb result holds in these discrete settings, with positive-quasiprobability pure states playing the role of minimal-uncertainty states, and KD nonpositivity is quantitatively tied to increased uncertainty.

title: Gaussian Quantum Integrated Sensing and Communication
summary: We consider a quantum integrated sensing and communication problem over an optical link in which a low-power transmitter simultaneously communicates with a receiver and identifies the range of a defect producing a backscattered signal. We model the system as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, in which the target, modeled as a beamsplitter, affects the timing of the backscattered signal through its location. Motivated by the envisioned deployment of entanglement-enabled quantum networks, we develop two protocols that allow the transmitter to leverage shared Gaussian entanglement, in the form of independent two-mode squeezed vacuum states or coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum states, to assist both sensing and communication. Since entanglement is known to enhance sensing, as demonstrated in quantum illumination, and to increase communication rates through entanglement-assisted communication, the transmitter faces a trade-off in allocating its entanglement resources between the two tasks. Our main results characterize these trade-offs under the proposed protocols in terms of achievable communication rate/sensing error-exponent regions, which outperform time-sharing schemes and demonstrate a quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a quantum integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) problem over a lossy thermal-noise bosonic optical link, where a low-power transmitter both communicates with a receiver and estimates the range of a backscattering defect. Two entanglement-assisted protocols are proposed and their communication-rate/sensing-error-exponent trade-offs are characterized, showing gains over time-sharing and a quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Entanglement is known to enhance sensing (quantum illumination) and to boost communication rates (entanglement-assisted communication). When a single low-power transmitter must perform both tasks simultaneously, it must split a limited entanglement resource between sensing and communication, creating an inherent trade-off that needs to be quantified. The work is motivated by envisioned deployments of entanglement-enabled quantum networks.
AI.method: The system is modeled as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel with a target modeled as a beamsplitter whose location determines the timing (delay) of the backscattered signal. Two protocols are developed that let the transmitter exploit shared Gaussian entanglement: (i) independent two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) states and (ii) coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum states, with entanglement allocated between the communication and sensing sub-tasks.
AI.result: The trade-offs under both protocols are characterized as achievable regions of communication rate versus sensing error exponent. These regions outperform time-sharing schemes between separate sensing and communication, demonstrating a quantum advantage.
AI.conclusion: Shared Gaussian entanglement can jointly assist sensing and communication in a quantum ISAC setting, and the proposed two-mode and three-mode squeezed-state protocols yield rate–error-exponent regions that exceed time-sharing baselines, confirming a quantum advantage in the entanglement-allocation trade-off.

title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis
summary:
In Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) using surface codes, reducing $T$-count is critical for efficient computation due to the high cost of $T$-state distillation. Probabilistic Quantum Circuit with Fallback (PQF) synthesis significantly lowers $T$-counts compared to standard protocols like Gridsynth, but introduces high circuit dynamism through extra gates inserted at runtime. This dynamism invalidates static compile-time routing, as these new $T$ gates require dynamic lattice surgery routing to establish non-intersecting ancilla paths to $T$-state factories while minimizing total execution time.
  To address this, we introduce $\text{R}^2$-PQF, a Runtime Routing protocol for PQF-synthesized quantum circuits. $\text{R}^2$-PQF dynamically routes gates layer-by-layer, computing paths during the execution of the previous logical timestep. To satisfy the strict computational window of $\sim t_{lattice\_surgery} + t_{reaction}$ and non-intersectionality constraints, we implement a Wavefront Breadth-First Search (W-BFS) and synthesise it on a 500MHz FPGA and 2 GHz ASIC. For a clock cycle of 2GHz, we achieve a median logical time-step of $1.51 μs$ for a 300 qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit, demonstrating that $\text{R}^2$-PQF successfully resolves the vast majority of paths (with rare exceptions) within the execution window and enables the $T$-count benefits of PQF without latency penalties. Compared to a baseline stalling-based solution (the only no-runtime-recomputation solution), $\text{R}^2$-PQF speeds up circuit execution by $1.34\times$ on average and up to $1.76 \times$.

AI.tldr: R²-PQF is a runtime routing protocol that dynamically computes lattice-surgery paths for PQF-synthesized surface-code circuits within the execution window, preserving PQF's low T-count without latency penalties.
AI.motivation: In FTQC with surface codes, T-count reduction is critical because T-state distillation is expensive. PQF synthesis lowers T-counts versus Gridsynth but inserts extra runtime gates, creating circuit dynamism that invalidates static compile-time routing; these runtime T gates need dynamic lattice-surgery routing for non-intersecting ancilla paths to T-state factories while minimizing execution time.
AI.method: The authors propose R²-PQF, which routes gates layer-by-layer and computes paths during execution of the previous logical timestep to hide routing latency. To meet the strict computational window (~t_lattice_surgery + t_reaction) and non-intersectionality constraints, they use a Wavefront Breadth-First Search (W-BFS), synthesized on a 500 MHz FPGA and a 2 GHz ASIC.
AI.result: At a 2 GHz clock, R²-PQF achieves a median logical timestep of 1.51 μs for a 300-qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit, resolving the vast majority of paths within the execution window (with rare exceptions). Compared to a baseline stalling-based solution (the only no-runtime-recomputation approach), it speeds up circuit execution by 1.34× on average and up to 1.76×.
AI.conclusion: R²-PQF successfully enables the T-count benefits of PQF without latency penalties by dynamically resolving routing within the execution window using efficient W-BFS hardware.

title: Anti-distinguishability of quantum channels
summary: We study single-query perfect anti-distinguishability/exclusion tasks of finite quantum channel ensembles, primarily using associated Choi operators and process POVMs. Weak perfect anti-distinguishability requires each measurement outcome to exclude an ensemble candidate with certainty, whereas the strong form additionally requires every candidate to have an exclusion outcome occurring with non-zero probability. For pairs of channels, both coincide with perfect distinguishability, whereas larger ensembles exhibit separations. We derive Choi-operator-support-based obstructions: weak exclusion requires at least two rank-deficient Choi operators, while strong exclusion requires the support of every candidate Choi operator to be strictly contained in the joint Choi support. The common Choi support must also lie in the kernel of the PPOVM normalisation. For commuting Choi operators, this condition is sufficient for weak exclusion when the normalisation also commutes with them. Conversely, a nonzero admixture of the same noise channel into every candidate precludes weak exclusion for any probe. We apply these results to measure-and-prepare, state-space contraction, Pauli, and replacer channels. In particular, the full permutation-channel ensemble of an unlabeled POVM is strongly anti-distinguishable exactly when some POVM effect is rank-deficient, while replacer-channel exclusion reduces to state exclusion. A Choi-commuting ensemble exhibits strong exclusion with an unassisted probe although no positive-definite PPOVM normalisation permits even weak exclusion. In contrast, commuting qubit phase gates, whose Choi operators need not commute, admit exact convex-hull criteria for weak and strong exclusion, both attainable without assistance.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes single-query perfect anti-distinguishability/exclusion of finite quantum channel ensembles via Choi operators and process POVMs, distinguishing weak (each outcome excludes a candidate with certainty) from strong (every candidate has an exclusion outcome occurring with non-zero probability) exclusion, and derives support-based obstructions, commuting-Choi sufficiency conditions, noise-admixture no-go results, and exact criteria for qubit phase-gate ensembles.
AI.motivation: Perfect distinguishability of quantum channels is well studied, but the complementary task of perfectly excluding (anti-distinguishing) channel candidates in a single query is less understood; the authors aim to establish structural criteria and separations between weak and strong exclusion for finite channel ensembles using the Choi/process-POVM framework.
AI.method: The analysis uses Choi operators of the channels and process POVMs (PPOVMs) with a normalisation operator. For pairs, anti-distinguishability is shown to coincide with perfect distinguishability, while larger ensembles separate the weak and strong notions. Support-based obstructions are derived: weak exclusion requires at least two rank-deficient Choi operators, and strong exclusion requires each candidate's Choi support to be strictly contained in the joint Choi support; the common Choi support must lie in the kernel of the PPOVM normalisation. For commuting Choi operators, this condition is sufficient for weak exclusion when the normalisation commutes with them. A nonzero admixture of a common noise channel into every candidate is shown to preclude weak exclusion for any probe. These results are applied to measure-and-prepare, state-space contraction, Pauli, replacer, permutation, and commuting qubit phase-gate channel ensembles.
AI.result: Support-based necessary conditions separate weak from strong exclusion; for commuting Choi operators the support condition becomes sufficient for weak exclusion under a commuting normalisation; common-noise admixture makes weak exclusion impossible; the full permutation-channel ensemble of an unlabeled POVM is strongly anti-distinguishable iff some POVM effect is rank-deficient; replacer-channel exclusion reduces to state exclusion; a Choi-commuting ensemble admits strong exclusion with an unassisted probe although no positive-definite PPOVM normalisation allows even weak exclusion; and commuting qubit phase gates admit exact convex-hull criteria for both weak and strong exclusion, attainable without assistance.
AI.conclusion: Perfect anti-distinguishability of channel ensembles is governed by Choi-operator support structure and PPOVM normalisation constraints, yielding clean obstructions, sufficiency results for commuting families, and a common-noise no-go theorem; the framework unifies channel exclusion with state exclusion and provides exact, assistance-free criteria for important channel classes.

title: Entanglement Allocation for Quantum Integrated Sensing and Communication
summary:
Jointly supporting communication and distributed sensing over a shared, limited pool of entanglement resources is an attractive prospect for future quantum networks. We develop a network-level quantum integrated sensing and communication (Q-ISAC) framework in which a quantum base station dynamically allocates elementary Bell pairs between communication users and distributed sensing. Sensing resources are adaptively partitioned among multiple GHZ probes with dynamically selected sizes and sensing-node assignments. We derive an effective quantum Fisher information model accounting for probabilistic fusion, transmission loss, and memory decoherence, and formulate a finite-horizon allocation problem subject to communication QoS, expected sensing-information, sensing-reliability, and hardware constraints. A hierarchical constrained proximal policy optimization (HC-PPO) framework combines learned discrete sensing allocation with analytical continuous communication allocation.
  Numerical results show that GHZ probing requires approximately $27$--30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest probe-size caps and 65-67% fewer at the highest considered target under the same sensing requirements. Adaptive multi-GHZ partitioning provides greater robustness than single-GHZ sensing, while adaptive communication--sensing sharing outperforms the evaluated fixed splits. The proposed HC-PPO framework satisfies the joint requirements in at least 99.9% of test instances across the considered sensing targets and fusion probabilities. Monte Carlo evaluation separately shows that realized terminal information reached its target in 96-98% of realizations, distinguishing expected-information satisfaction from realized sensing performance.

AI.tldr: A network-level quantum integrated sensing and communication (Q-ISAC) framework where a base station dynamically allocates shared Bell pairs between communication users and distributed GHZ-based sensing, solved via hierarchical constrained PPO (HC-PPO).
AI.motivation: Future quantum networks must jointly support communication and distributed sensing over a limited shared entanglement pool; how to adaptively allocate these scarce resources while meeting both communication QoS and sensing requirements is an open problem.
AI.method: Formulates dynamic allocation of elementary Bell pairs between communication users and distributed sensing, with sensing resources adaptively partitioned among multiple GHZ probes of selected sizes and node assignments. Derives an effective quantum Fisher information model incorporating probabilistic fusion, transmission loss, and memory decoherence; poses a finite-horizon allocation problem under communication QoS, expected sensing-information, sensing-reliability, and hardware constraints. HC-PPO combines learned discrete sensing allocation with analytical continuous communication allocation.
AI.result: GHZ probing needs ~27-30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest probe-size caps, and 65-67% fewer at the highest target. Adaptive multi-GHZ partitioning is more robust than single-GHZ sensing, and adaptive communication-sensing sharing beats fixed splits. HC-PPO meets joint requirements in at least 99.9% of test instances; Monte Carlo shows realized terminal information hits its target in 96-98% of realizations.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive entanglement allocation with multi-GHZ partitioning and HC-PPO enables efficient, reliable joint quantum sensing and communication, while distinguishing expected-information satisfaction from realized sensing performance.

title: Quantum identity authentication protocol via perturbed probability amplitudes
summary: Quantum identity authentication is an effective solution for establishing mutual trust between communicating parties in the post-quantum era. To address the risk of partial secret information leakage under special measurements, this paper designs a quantum identity authentication protocol based on perturbed probability amplitudes. The protocol first proposes a method of encoding a random sequence onto the probability amplitudes of quantum entangled states, forming perturbed probability amplitudes, thereby reducing the involvement of shared information between the sender and receiver. Furthermore, it presents a method for generating n-bit random authentication information based on the n-bit pre-shared information, enhancing the randomness of the authentication information relative to an attacker. The proposed protocol can resist impersonation attack, CNOT attack, and entanglement measurement attack, and ensures backward security. Under equivalent security conditions, the amount of shared information is 1/n that in Chen et al.'s scheme and half that in Dutta et al.'s scheme. And each bit of the secret message has no risk of leakage under special measurements. It can also be extended to a bi-directional quantum identity authentication protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum identity authentication protocol based on perturbed probability amplitudes, encoding random sequences onto the amplitudes of entangled states to reduce shared-information reliance and prevent partial secret leakage under special measurements.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum identity authentication schemes risk partial leakage of secret information under special measurements, and they require large amounts of pre-shared information between communicating parties.
AI.method: Encode a random sequence onto the probability amplitudes of quantum entangled states to form perturbed probability amplitudes, reducing shared-information involvement; generate n-bit random authentication information from n-bit pre-shared information to raise randomness against attackers.
AI.result: The protocol resists impersonation, CNOT, and entanglement measurement attacks and ensures backward security; shared information is 1/n of Chen et al.'s scheme and half of Dutta et al.'s under equivalent security, with no per-bit leakage risk under special measurements; extendable to bidirectional authentication.
AI.conclusion: The perturbed-probability-amplitude design yields a secure, information-efficient quantum identity authentication protocol with backward security and no special-measurement leakage, extensible to bidirectional settings.

title: Initialization-controlled fault sensitivity and force-balance plateaus in noisy variational quantum optimization
summary: We study deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain under local gate depolarization, at depths where noiseless training is coherently exact. Full-width initializations reach low coherent error faster than circuits with confined transverse generators, but incur a larger noise shift and need an order of magnitude more updates for noisy convergence. In many-body-localization-inspired initialization, bounding the initial transverse generator amplitudes keeps the operator support localized and suffices for low-fragility optimization, so longitudinal disorder and Floquet layer repetition are unnecessary. The fault-erasure fraction, the mean fraction of coherent energy removed per fault, sets the effective visibility through a parameter-free exponential model. Full-width circuits start with delocalized operator support, and once coherent energy builds up, each fault erases nearly all of it. Initially, their noise-induced gradient almost uniformly attenuates the coherent gradient, so coherent descent proceeds at the noiseless rate. They then stall on a high-noise force-balance plateau, where finite coherent and noise-induced gradients cancel to first order. At late times all initializations reach the same fault-erasure fraction and noisy-error band, but operator support contracts more slowly, at a rate set by the plateau residence time.

AI.tldr: Deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain under local gate depolarization are analyzed at noiselessly exact depths. Initialization geometry controls noise fragility via the fault-erasure fraction: full-width inits train coherently faster but converge noisily ~10x slower, while amplitude-bounded localized inits suffice for low-fragility optimization.
AI.motivation: To understand how initialization affects noise resilience of deep variational circuits (VQAs) in the coherently exact regime, and to identify what properties of many-body-localization-inspired initialization are actually necessary for low-fragility optimization.
AI.method: Variational circuit study of a periodic Heisenberg chain with local gate depolarization at depths where noiseless training is coherently exact. Compares full-width initializations versus transverse-generator-confined and MBL-inspired amplitude-bounded initializations. Introduces the fault-erasure fraction (mean coherent energy removed per fault) and a parameter-free exponential visibility model; tracks operator support, coherent vs noise-induced gradients, and a high-noise force-balance plateau.
AI.result: Full-width inits reach low coherent error faster but incur larger noise shift, require an order of magnitude more updates for noisy convergence, and start with delocalized operator support so each fault erases nearly all built-up coherent energy. Initially noise-induced gradients nearly uniformly attenuate coherent gradients, so coherent descent proceeds at the noiseless rate; circuits then stall on a high-noise force-balance plateau where finite coherent and noise-induced gradients cancel to first order. At late times all inits reach the same fault-erasure fraction and noisy-error band, but operator support contracts more slowly at a rate set by plateau residence time.
AI.conclusion: The fault-erasure fraction governs effective visibility via a parameter-free exponential model and links initialization geometry to noisy optimization dynamics. Bounding initial transverse generator amplitudes localizes operator support, sufficient for low-fragility optimization without needing longitudinal disorder or Floquet layer repetition.

title: Information-Geometric Representation of Upper Bounds on Fluctuation Growth in Open Quantum Systems
summary:
Building on our earlier results for closed quantum systems, we investigate the dynamical evolution of quantum fluctuations and their connections to Fisher information and the quantum operations describing open-system dynamics. Starting from a general expression for the time derivative of an observable's uncertainty, we derive an alternative upper bound on fluctuation growth in an open quantum system using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The resulting bound separates contributions from the evolution of the quantum state and the explicit time dependence of the observable, reducing to a known result for closed-system dynamics. We then establish a connection between fluctuation dynamics and quantum Fisher information by decomposing the density operator and the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) into coherent and incoherent contributions, which leads to a bound relating the evolution of observable uncertainty to the coherent and incoherent components of the Fisher information, providing an information-geometric interpretation of fluctuation growth.
  To connect fluctuation dynamics with quantum operations governing open-system evolutions, we derive the time evolution of the eigenvalues of the density operator in terms of Kraus operators. Using the infinitesimal-time relation between Kraus and Lindblad operators, we obtain a corresponding expression for the eigenvalue dynamics in terms of Lindblad operators. This formulation directly relates changes in the density operator eigenvalues to the quantum processes acting on the system. We then study the results using some examples. Our results provide a framework connecting observable fluctuation growth, Fisher information, and the Kraus and Lindblad descriptions of quantum evolution, offering a route toward understanding how specific quantum channels influence the information and fluctuations available in an evolving quantum system.

AI.tldr: The paper derives new bounds on the growth of observable uncertainty (quantum fluctuations) in open quantum systems, linking fluctuation dynamics to quantum Fisher information and to the Kraus/Lindblad descriptions of quantum channels.
AI.motivation: Extending earlier work on closed quantum systems, the authors seek to understand how fluctuation growth, information content (Fisher information), and the quantum operations that govern open-system dynamics are interrelated, providing an information-geometric view of fluctuations in open systems.
AI.method: Starting from the time derivative of an observable's uncertainty, they use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to derive an upper bound on fluctuation growth that separates state-evolution and observable time-dependence contributions. They decompose the density operator and symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) into coherent and incoherent parts to bound uncertainty evolution via coherent/incoherent Fisher information. They also derive eigenvalue dynamics of the density operator in terms of Kraus operators, then translate these to Lindblad operators via the infinitesimal-time relation, and illustrate with examples.
AI.result: The new Cauchy-Schwarz bound generalizes and reduces to the known closed-system result, separating state-evolution and observable-explicit-time contributions. A bound relates observable-uncertainty evolution to coherent and incoherent Fisher information components, giving an information-geometric interpretation of fluctuation growth. Eigenvalue dynamics are expressed in terms of Kraus operators and, equivalently, Lindblad operators, directly tying eigenvalue changes to the acting quantum processes.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified framework connecting observable fluctuation growth, quantum Fisher information, and Kraus/Lindblad descriptions of open-system evolution, offering a route to understand how specific quantum channels affect available information and fluctuations in an evolving quantum system.

title: Reasoning about Shared-Qubit Concurrency in Quantum Computing
summary: In this paper, we develop a semantic model for the parallel execution of quantum circuits, providing a formal foundation for studying shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing. As in classical shared-memory concurrency, parallel quantum circuits may interfere with one another through operations on shared qubits. However, quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations introduce additional challenges for reasoning about their correctness. To address these challenges, we generalise the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum computing at the level of quantum circuits. Our approach enables compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits by separating the verification of individual components from the analysis of interference between them. We formulate proof rules for establishing the correctness of parallel quantum circuits and prove their soundness with respect to the proposed semantic model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a semantic model for parallel quantum circuits and generalizes the Owicki-Gries method to enable compositional, interference-aware reasoning about shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Parallel quantum circuits, like classical shared-memory concurrent programs, can interfere through operations on shared qubits. Quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations add challenges beyond classical concurrency, making correctness reasoning difficult.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal semantic model for parallel quantum circuit execution and generalize the classical Owicki-Gries method to the quantum circuit level. They formulate proof rules that separate verification of individual circuit components from analysis of interference between them, and prove soundness of the rules with respect to the semantic model.
AI.result: Compositional proof rules for establishing correctness of parallel quantum circuits, together with a soundness proof relative to the proposed semantic model.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a formal foundation for reasoning about shared-qubit concurrency in quantum circuits, enabling compositional verification that handles entanglement and noncommutativity.

title: An example of universal braiding in Links--Gould topological quantum computation
summary: We construct a universal quantum computational encoding via braiding in Links--Gould fusion spaces associated to $U_q^H(\mathfrak{sl}(2|1))$ where $q$ is on the unit circle and is not a root of unity. The construction uses only neglectons and is realized in the morphism spaces $\mathrm{Hom}_{U_q^H}(V(0,α),V(0,-\frac{1}{2})^{\otimes 2N}\otimes V(0,α)).$ Under explicit positivity and arithmetic constraints these spaces admit a $2^N$-dimensional computational subspace with a positive definite Hermitian form. We prove single-qubit density in $\mathrm{U}(2,1)$ and approximate arbitrary unitary operators on $N$-qubit computational subspaces with arbitrarily small leakage. The calculations use explicit inclusions, projections, and Hermitian pairings without requiring $F$-matrices.

AI.tldr: A universal quantum computational encoding is built via braiding in Links–Gould fusion spaces of $U_q^H(\mathfrak{sl}(2|1))$ (non-root-of-unity $q$ on the unit circle), using only neglectons to obtain $2^N$-dimensional computational subspaces supporting universal quantum computation.
AI.motivation: To realize quantum computation topologically through braiding of anyonic excitations, one needs fusion spaces that carry a well-defined finite-dimensional computational subspace with a positive definite inner product and support universal gates.
AI.method: Construction of a universal encoding via braiding in Links–Gould fusion spaces associated with $U_q^H(\mathfrak{sl}(2|1))$, $q$ on the unit circle and not a root of unity. Uses only neglectons, realized in morphism spaces $\mathrm{Hom}_{U_q^H}(V(0,\alpha),V(0,-\tfrac{1}{2})^{\otimes 2N}\otimes V(0,\alpha))$. Under explicit positivity and arithmetic constraints these spaces admit a $2^N$-dimensional computational subspace with positive definite Hermitian form. Calculations rely on explicit inclusions, projections, and Hermitian pairings, avoiding $F$-matrices.
AI.result: Single-qubit gates are shown to be dense in $\mathrm{U}(2,1)$, and arbitrary unitary operators on $N$-qubit computational subspaces can be approximated with arbitrarily small leakage.
AI.conclusion: The Links–Gould fusion spaces of $U_q^H(\mathfrak{sl}(2|1))$ with neglecton braiding furnish a viable universal quantum computational encoding, with universality established via density in $\mathrm{U}(2,1)$ and leakage-controlled approximation, without resorting to $F$-matrices.

title: Approximate Synthetic Spectra of Quantum Systems Associated with Compact Lie Groups
summary: How can noncommuting quantum observables retain the geometry of a classical phase space? Motivated by Mumford's question on approximately macroscopically unique (AMU) states and the work of Lin and Wang, we study synthetic spectra of position--momentum and angular-momentum systems. Under the hypotheses of their AMU theorems, nonempty synthetic spectra yield AMU states. For sufficiently small $\hbar$, the position--momentum spectrum fills the plane, while the angular-momentum spectrum contains any prescribed ball. The latter calculation leads to compact Lie groups: we prove that highest-weight coadjoint orbits lie in regional synthetic spectra under an explicit variance bound. Function-space representations of $SU(n)$, $SO(n)$, and $Sp(n)$ provide further examples.

AI.tldr: Under the AMU (approximately macroscopically unique) hypotheses of Lin--Wang, nonempty synthetic spectra produce AMU states; for small ℏ the position–momentum synthetic spectrum fills the plane and the angular-momentum spectrum contains any prescribed ball, and highest-weight coadjoint orbits of compact Lie groups lie in regional synthetic spectra under an explicit variance bound, with examples from function-space representations of SU(n), SO(n), Sp(n).
AI.motivation: Mumford's question on approximately macroscopically unique (AMU) states asks how noncommuting quantum observables can nonetheless retain a classical phase-space-like geometry; the work builds on Lin and Wang's AMU theorems to make this precise via synthetic spectra of position–momentum and angular-momentum systems.
AI.method: Synthetic spectra are studied for position–momentum and angular-momentum systems under the hypotheses of the Lin–Wang AMU theorems: nonempty synthetic spectra are shown to yield AMU states; semiclassical (small-ℏ) analysis of the position–momentum spectrum; a computation for angular momentum yielding prescribed balls; extension to compact Lie groups proving highest-weight coadjoint orbits lie in regional synthetic spectra under an explicit variance bound; and function-space representations of SU(n), SO(n), Sp(n) as further examples.
AI.result: Nonempty synthetic spectra imply AMU states under the AMU hypotheses. For sufficiently small ℏ, the position–momentum synthetic spectrum fills the plane, and the angular-momentum synthetic spectrum contains any prescribed ball. For compact Lie groups, highest-weight coadjoint orbits lie in regional synthetic spectra subject to an explicit variance bound, and function-space representations of SU(n), SO(n), Sp(n) supply additional examples.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic spectra offer a coherent framework linking noncommuting quantum observables to classical phase-space geometry: they characterize AMU states, recover full-plane/ball semiclassical structure, and extend to compact Lie groups via highest-weight coadjoint orbits and classical matrix-group representations.

title: A Conditional Quantum Kac-Bernstein Theorem
summary: We establish a conditional quantum Kac-Bernstein theorem for mixing of two independent, finite-mode bosonic inputs with quantum memories. We characterize exactly when the outputs are conditionally independent given both memories. Each input then decomposes into orthogonal memory sectors sharing a common Gaussian state on the physical system and a bosonic memory factor, up to sector-dependent physical displacements.
