In particular, triviality of the common bosonic factor implies separability of the inputs, as occurs whenever either memory has finite-dimensional support.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a conditional quantum Kac-Bernstein theorem for two independent finite-mode bosonic inputs with quantum memories, giving an exact characterization of when mixing outputs become conditionally independent given the memories.
AI.motivation: The classical Kac-Bernstein theorem characterizes when a mixture of independent random variables yields independent outputs; its quantum analogue for continuous-variable bosonic systems with quantum memory remained open, and understanding the structure of such mixtures is key for quantum information and mixing problems.
AI.method: Analyze a mixing map acting on two independent finite-mode bosonic inputs, each carrying a quantum memory. Characterize conditional independence of the outputs given both memories, decomposing each input into orthogonal memory sectors with a common Gaussian state on the physical system, a bosonic memory factor, and sector-dependent physical displacements.
AI.result: Exact characterization: outputs are conditionally independent given the memories iff each input decomposes into orthogonal memory sectors sharing a common Gaussian state (up to sector-dependent displacements) and a bosonic memory factor. Triviality of the common bosonic factor implies separability of the inputs, which occurs whenever either memory has finite-dimensional support.
AI.conclusion: The work extends the Kac-Bernstein characterization to the quantum bosonic setting with memory, providing structural constraints on conditionally independent mixtures and linking bosonic-memory triviality to input separability.

title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
summary:
Quantum circuit optimization is an indispensable component of the quantum software stack, used to reduce noise, maximize performance, alleviate costs of quantum error correction, or target specific hardware. A related problem is approximate membership: for a fixed set of unitaries $S$, decide whether a given circuit $C$ is within distance $\varepsilon$ of a unitary in $S$ under some metric $m$. Membership is a special case of optimization, where $S$ is a set of unitaries implementable at no cost (e.g., with noise-minimal circuits, or without magic states). Janzing, Wocjan, and Beth (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2005) showed that, for the operator metric, the case $S=\{I\}$ (approximate identity) is QMA-complete when $C$ is promised to be either close to the identity or far from it.
  We generalize this setting in three directions: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) besides $S=\{I\}$, sets $S$ containing only Clifford unitaries, or only generalized permutation matrices (i.e., no superposition), and (iii) the trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. We show that, in all cases, approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of $\varepsilon$, provided $C$'s gate-set can implement Clifford+T, as the gate-sets of standard hardware do. If $S=\{I\}$, or if $S$ contains only generalized permutation matrices, $I\in S$, and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial $\varepsilon$. If $S=\{I\}$ and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds even for circuits over classical-reversible gate-sets.
  Our results indicate that approximate membership is harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and that this hardness persists across quantum resources (any gates, non-Clifford, superposition) and distance metrics. They directly imply PP-hardness of circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that approximate membership of a circuit to a set of unitaries S is PP-hard (under promise-free inputs, Clifford-only or generalized-permutation sets, and trace/spectral/operator metrics), implying PP-hardness of circuit optimization for total, non-Clifford, and superposition gate depth/count.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuit optimization and approximate membership are central to reducing noise and costs. Prior work (Janzing, Wocjan, Beth 2005) only established QMA-completeness for the special case S={I} under the operator metric with a promise; the general, promise-free, multi-metric, and multi-set landscape remained open.
AI.method: Generalize approximate membership along three axes: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) sets S = {I}, Clifford-only sets, or sets of generalized permutation matrices, and (iii) operator, spectral, and trace-based metrics. Analyze hardness assuming the circuit gate-set can implement Clifford+T; also consider classical-reversible gate-sets for the {I} trace-based case.
AI.result: Approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of ε in all cases; for S={I} or permutation-only S with I∈S under trace-based metrics, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial ε, and for S={I} with trace metrics even over classical-reversible gate-sets.
AI.conclusion: Approximate membership is strictly harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and this hardness persists across quantum resources and metrics, directly yielding PP-hardness of circuit optimization for total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth/count.

title: Reducing the arithmetic cost of quantum derivative pricing with language-model circuit design
summary:
Quantum amplitude estimation can estimate expected discounted payoffs with quadratically fewer oracle calls than Monte Carlo, but each call requires coherent computation. We use language-model-assisted circuit design to reduce reversible payoff arithmetic for a three-asset worst-of autocallable and a target accrual redemption forward (TARF). The constructions retain compact integer representations of market paths alongside contract history, reconstructing quantities temporarily for contract decisions and payoff-angle evaluation.
  Relative to matched internal references, the factor-sum autocallable and windowed TARF circuits reduce the product of Toffoli count and peak logical qubits $(N_{Tof} Q_{max})$ by factors of 2.39 and 4.84, respectively. At a second autocallable setting, fresh search recovers a 1.35-fold saving after the tested fixed adaptation loses its advantage. For the factor-sum circuit, we prove exact coherent execution of its integer specification for every input, incoming accumulator and measurement record, with clean workspace and phase cancellation. A separate lattice calculation gives a numerical angle-tolerance-violation probability of 6.248e-8 and evaluates pricing bias under the declared loading law, with bounded omission but no certified numerical enclosure. The results connect compact representations to lower-cost payoff arithmetic and separately assessed logical and financial correctness. Their resource scope excludes loading, payoff rotation and estimation.

AI.tldr: Language-model-assisted circuit design cuts reversible payoff arithmetic cost (Toffoli×qubits) by 2.39× and 4.84× for a worst-of autocallable and a windowed TARF, with proven exact coherent execution for the autocallable circuit.
AI.motivation: Quantum amplitude estimation offers quadratic oracle-call savings over Monte Carlo for discounted payoff estimation, but each oracle call must be computed coherently, making reversible payoff arithmetic the dominant cost. The work targets reducing that arithmetic overhead for realistic structured products.
AI.method: Uses language-model-assisted circuit design to build compact integer representations of market paths plus contract history, reconstructing quantities only temporarily for contract decisions and payoff-angle evaluation. Applies to a three-asset worst-of autocallable (factor-sum construction) and a target accrual redemption forward (windowed construction), benchmarked against matched internal references, with fresh search tested after a fixed adaptation degrades. Formal proof of exact coherent execution (all inputs, incoming accumulator, measurement record; clean workspace, phase cancellation) plus a separate lattice calculation of angle-tolerance-violation probability and pricing bias.
AI.result: N_Tof·Q_max reduced by factors of 2.39 (factor-sum autocallable) and 4.84 (windowed TARF); a fresh search recovers 1.35× saving at a second autocallable setting where the fixed adaptation loses advantage. Lattice calculation yields angle-tolerance-violation probability 6.248e-8; pricing bias evaluated with bounded omission but no certified numerical enclosure.
AI.conclusion: Compact integer representations enable lower-cost payoff arithmetic, and logical correctness (proven coherent execution) is assessed separately from financial correctness (angle tolerance, pricing bias). Resource scope excludes state loading, payoff rotation, and estimation.

title: Universal Free-Electron-Sideband Control
summary: Advances in free-electron quantum optics are establishing free electrons as a versatile quantum resource. Photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) interactions and free drift provide elementary operations for shaping the longitudinal electron wavefunction, yet their full control capabilities remain unexplored. Here, we prove that a finite sequence of alternating monochromatic PINEM interactions and free drifts can approximate any prescribed inner-product-preserving map from a finite-dimensional input subspace into the full ideal electron-sideband Hilbert space to arbitrary accuracy. We therefore call the protocol PINEMAD (PINEM And Drift). This framework encompasses state preparation, unitary gates, and isometric encoding. We further show numerically that parameter optimization enables high-fidelity state preparation at finite electron energy spreads, using experimentally accessible coupling strengths and tabletop-scale total drift lengths. These results establish electron energy sidebands as a programmable quantum resource.

AI.tldr: Finite alternating sequences of monochromatic PINEM interactions and free drifts (PINEMAD) are proven universal for approximating any inner-product-preserving map from a finite-dimensional subspace into the full electron-sideband Hilbert space, enabling programmable electron-sideband quantum processing.
AI.motivation: PINEM interactions and free drift are known elementary operations for shaping the longitudinal electron wavefunction, but whether they suffice for full control over the electron-sideband Hilbert space had not been established. The authors aim to close this gap and establish free electrons as a programmable quantum resource.
AI.method: The protocol alternates monochromatic PINEM interactions with free drifts (PINEMAD). The paper proves a universality theorem: any prescribed inner-product-preserving (isometric) map from a finite-dimensional input subspace into the full ideal electron-sideband Hilbert space can be approximated to arbitrary accuracy by a finite PINEMAD sequence. Numerical parameter optimization is used to assess state preparation under realistic finite electron energy spread.
AI.result: PINEMAD is shown to be universal, subsuming state preparation, unitary gates, and isometric encoding as special cases. Numerical optimization demonstrates high-fidelity state preparation despite finite electron energy spread, using experimentally accessible coupling strengths and tabletop-scale total drift lengths.
AI.conclusion: Alternating PINEM and free-drift sequences provide universal control of longitudinal electron wavefunctions, establishing electron energy sidebands as a programmable quantum resource and a viable platform for quantum information tasks such as state preparation, gates, and isometric encoding.

title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture for Image Reconstruction
summary: We introduce the Pauli-Correlator Autoencoder (PCAE), a hybrid quantum--classical architecture for image reconstruction. PCAE splits an image into patches and compresses each patch as a matrix product state (MPS). A small quantum circuit turns each compressed patch into a few measured numbers, and a classical neural network rebuilds the patch from these numbers and the patch position. A learnable energy term, taken from physics, is added to training and tracked as training proceeds. Two versions place the six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or on a grid (PCAE2D). An averaging step makes the PCAE2D features follow rotations and reflections of the image exactly. Trained on one image at a time, PCAE2D rebuilds images from six public datasets with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 25.8 to 41.6 decibels. On CIFAR-10 images not used in training, a formula-based stand-in for the PCAE2D features performs within 1 decibel of several simpler classical methods. Five trained models also run on real IBM quantum computers without retraining, and rebuild images at 25.90 to 31.52 decibels. A short argument and a synthetic test show that, with a linear final layer, measuring qubits in pairs is needed for targets built from products of inputs. These results show that PCAE works as a hybrid model that rebuilds varied images and runs on today's quantum hardware at the six-qubit scale.

AI.tldr: PCAE is a hybrid quantum-classical autoencoder that compresses image patches as MPS, encodes each in a six-qubit circuit with measured Pauli correlators, and reconstructs patches via a classical decoder, achieving 25.8–41.6 dB PSNR and running on real IBM hardware.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to establish a practical hybrid quantum-classical image reconstruction model that (i) exploits compact tensor-network (MPS) patch representations, (ii) uses few qubits and measured observables to produce classical features, and (iii) is deployable on current quantum hardware while remaining competitive with simple classical baselines.
AI.method: Images are split into patches, each compressed into an MPS. A small quantum circuit maps each compressed patch to a few measured Pauli correlator expectation values; a classical network reconstructs the patch from these features plus patch position. A learnable physics-inspired energy term is added to the loss and tracked during training. Two variants place six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or a grid (PCAE2D); PCAE2D averages features to achieve exact equivariance to rotations and reflections. Models are trained per-image. A theoretical argument plus synthetic tests analyze pair-wise qubit measurement requirements for product-structured targets with a linear final layer.
AI.result: PCAE2D reconstructs images from six public datasets at 25.8–41.6 dB PSNR on training images. On held-out CIFAR-10 images, a formula-based surrogate for PCAE2D features is within 1 dB of several simpler classical methods. Five trained models run on real IBM quantum computers without retraining, yielding 25.90–31.52 dB. Analysis shows that, with a linear final layer, pair-wise qubit measurements are necessary for targets built from products of inputs.
AI.conclusion: PCAE is a viable hybrid model that reconstructs diverse images and executes on present-day six-qubit quantum hardware, with feature equivariance and measurement-design insights supporting its design.

title: Broken-Symmetry Reference States for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization with Near-DMRG Accuracy
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23064186 (FCIDUMPs and raw quantum-hardware sample pools)
summary: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) accuracy remains limited for strongly correlated systems like iron-sulfur clusters. This accuracy heavily depends on the mean-field reference state, which determines the sampling ansatz and configuration-recovery target. We extend the qcsc-prefect workflow to support a broken-symmetry unrestricted Hartree-Fock (BS-UHF) starting point, derived from atom-localized antiferromagnetic initial guesses. For the $[Fe_4S_4(SCH_3)_4]^{2-}$ cubane (54 electrons, 36 orbitals, 72 data qubits; 88 total qubits), this lowers the mean-field reference by $\approx 534$ mHa relative to the Restricted Hartree-Fock (RHF) solution (-327.0809 vs. -326.5474 Ha). Combined with deep multi-step configuration recovery on ROQUO GPU nodes at subspace dimension $d = 3 \times 10^{10}$, we reach $E = -327.235076$ Ha. This is 4.3 mHa above the finite-$D = 4000$ DMRG value (-327.2393952 Ha) and $\sim 512-517$ mHa below a previous same-active-space RHF-reference SQD calculation. Extrapolating to the $d \to \infty$ limit via a Gaussian-in-log $d$ fitting ansatz gives an asymptotic estimate $E_\infty = -327.244468$ Ha $\pm 1.05$ mHa, just 0.33 mHa above our discarded-weight-extrapolated DMRG estimate ($E_{D\to\infty} = -327.244797$ Ha $\pm 0.46$ mHa), well within their combined $1σ$ uncertainty. We characterize the determinant-subspace composition driving convergence, show matching validation on $[Fe_2S_2(SCH_3)_4]^{2-}$, and report multi-HPC execution on Fugaku, Miyabi-G, and ROQUO. We conclude that reference-state preparation, rather than subspace size alone, is a key driver of SQD energy accuracy under strong electronic correlation.

AI.tldr: Extending sample-based quantum diagonalization with a broken-symmetry UHF reference state dramatically improves accuracy for strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters, reaching within ~0.3 mHa of extrapolated DMRG at an extrapolated limit.
AI.motivation: SQD accuracy for strongly correlated systems like iron-sulfur clusters is limited and depends heavily on the mean-field reference state, which sets both the sampling ansatz and the configuration-recovery target.
AI.method: Extends the qcsc-prefect workflow to support a broken-symmetry unrestricted Hartree-Fock (BS-UHF) reference derived from atom-localized antiferromagnetic initial guesses, combined with deep multi-step configuration recovery on ROQUO GPU nodes at subspace dimension d = 3×10^10. Uses a Gaussian-in-log-d fitting ansatz for d→∞ extrapolation and characterizes the determinant-subspace composition.
AI.result: For the [Fe4S4(SCH3)4]2- cubane (54 e-, 36 orbitals, 72 data qubits; 88 total), BS-UHF lowers the reference by ~534 mHa vs RHF (-327.0809 vs -326.5474 Ha). Reaches E = -327.235076 Ha, 4.3 mHa above finite-D=4000 DMRG (-327.2393952 Ha) and ~512-517 mHa below prior same-active-space RHF-reference SQD. Extrapolated E∞ = -327.244468 Ha ± 1.05 mHa, only 0.33 mHa above discarded-weight-extrapolated DMRG (E_{D→∞} = -327.244797 Ha ± 0.46 mHa), within combined 1σ. Validated on [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2-; executed on Fugaku, Miyabi-G, and ROQUO.
AI.conclusion: Reference-state preparation, rather than subspace size alone, is a key driver of SQD energy accuracy under strong electronic correlation.

title: Motional Decoherence of the internal state of an atom by vacuum and thermal fluctuations of a quantum field: Necessity of a fully relativistic treatment
summary: We consider a massive object, such as a neutral atom or an Unruh-DeWitt detector, moving at constant speed in a quantum field and investigate how motion affects the quantum coherence of its internal degrees of freedom, manifesting as quantum dispersion in the absence of a quantum field, and decoherence in its presence. Our investigation aims to serve two purposes: One is to obtain the correct results for these effects, which are essential for the design of quantum information processing schemes where the quantum coherence of an atom's internal degrees of freedom is of major concern. The other is to expose the fallacies in commonplace approaches, which start with a non-relativistic calculation and then add on relativistic ``corrections". We first show a fully relativistic calculation of the internal dynamics based on covariance principles, and then one which ignores these principles, often justified by the atom's slow motion. By a direct comparison of results from these two approaches, we identify {significant discrepancies} in a non-relativistic treatment, even at low atomic speeds. The proper procedure, and a much safer one in terms of accuracy, is recommended here: first derive the dynamics and the necessary regularizations within a fully covariant relativistic framework. Only after the exact, internally consistent equations of motion are established should low-velocity limits be extracted from them. Only in this way can all the relativistic effects which matter: time dilation, aberration, non-inertial mass shifts, be systematically preserved, and accurate results obtained.

AI.tldr: A fully covariant relativistic treatment of a slowly moving atom (or Unruh-DeWitt detector) coupled to a quantum field is shown to be necessary; the common "non-relativistic plus relativistic corrections" approach yields significant discrepancies even at low speeds.
AI.motivation: Quantum coherence of an atom's internal degrees of freedom is critical for quantum information processing, so accurate predictions of motional quantum dispersion (no field) and decoherence (with field) are needed. Additionally, the authors aim to expose fallacies in prevalent approaches that begin with a non-relativistic calculation and then append relativistic "corrections."
AI.method: The internal dynamics of a massive object moving at constant velocity in a quantum field is computed twice: once with a fully relativistic calculation based on covariance principles, and once with a method ignoring those principles (justified by slow motion). The two sets of results are compared directly.
AI.result: Direct comparison reveals significant discrepancies in the non-relativistic treatment, even at low atomic speeds, since effects such as time dilation, aberration, and non-inertial mass shifts are not systematically captured.
AI.conclusion: The proper and safer procedure is to first derive the dynamics and required regularizations within a fully covariant relativistic framework, then extract low-velocity limits from the exact, internally consistent equations of motion. This systematically preserves all relevant relativistic effects and yields accurate results.

title: Long-lived quantum memories with rare-earth ions doped in crystals
comment: The incorrect value 4.14 on page 7 of the published version has been corrected to 1.16
summary: Quantum memory is a core enabling device for large-scale quantum networks, serving as the fundamental building block for quantum repeaters and transportable quantum memories. Among various physical platforms, rare-earth-ion-doped crystals stand out as one of the most promising solid-state candidates for long-lived photonic quantum memories, owing to their exceptionally long spin coherence time and their compatibility with integration. In this review, we first introduce the physical mechanisms underlying long-lived spin coherence in rare-earth systems, with particular emphasis on the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling techniques. We then review the experimental progress in this field, highlighting three distinct lifetimes--the spin coherence time, the light storage time, and the quantum storage time--and covering experiments that have achieved hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges that hinder the realization of practical long-lived quantum memories, explore potential strategies to overcome these obstacles, and outline the prospects for their future applications in quantum networks.

AI.tldr: A review of rare-earth-ion-doped crystals as long-lived photonic quantum memories, covering physical mechanisms (zero-first-order-Zeeman transitions, dynamical decoupling) and experimental progress across spin coherence, light storage, and quantum storage lifetimes, plus remaining challenges and prospects for quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Quantum memory is a core enabling device for large-scale quantum networks, underpinning quantum repeaters and transportable quantum memories. Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals are among the most promising solid-state platforms due to exceptionally long spin coherence times and integration compatibility.
AI.method: Review/tutorial synthesis rather than a single experiment: first, explanation of physical mechanisms for long-lived spin coherence in rare-earth systems, emphasizing the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling; second, a survey of experimental progress organized around three distinct lifetimes (spin coherence time, light storage time, quantum storage time).
AI.result: The reviewed experiments report hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage.
AI.conclusion: Practical long-lived quantum memories still face remaining challenges; the review discusses strategies to overcome them and outlines prospects for future applications in quantum networks.

title: Decoy-state quantum key distribution with a leaky Mach-Zehnder receiver
summary: We prove the security of phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution for a Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors that leak fine-grained information about the detection patterns. For this, we derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combine it with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers. The leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, providing a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even in the presence of beam-splitter imbalance. Our results provide a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.

AI.tldr: The paper proves security of phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 QKD for an imperfect Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and leaky threshold detectors, deriving a loss-independent phase-error correction.
AI.motivation: Practical QKD receivers are imperfect: beam splitters are imbalanced and threshold detectors can leak fine-grained information about detection patterns. Existing security proofs typically assume ideal, symmetric, non-leaky receivers, so a loss-tolerant treatment accounting for receiver leakage is needed.
AI.method: The authors derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combine it with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers, applied to a Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors.
AI.result: A security proof is obtained in which the leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, yielding a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even under beam-splitter imbalance.
AI.conclusion: The results offer a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.

title: Wigner-Function Fingerprints of Collective Excitations in Mirror-Terminated Waveguide QED
summary: We investigate the emission profiles of singly excited collective states and propose a matched-mode witnessing protocol in a mirror-terminated waveguide quantum electrodynamics system. The amplitudes and relative phases of the initial collective excitation are encoded in the temporal mode of the emitted single-photon wavepacket, providing a route to state verification through the common waveguide output. We identify the emission mode associated with a chosen target state and employ an auxiliary virtual-cavity representation to evaluate the quantum state of this selected output mode. For a matched initial state, the selected mode contains the emitted single photon, whose Wigner function exhibits a pronounced non-classical negative dip, serving as a distinct fingerprint of the target many-body state. With the reference mode held fixed, different initial configurations yield different photon occupations and phase-space distributions, demonstrating the state selectivity of the protocol. These results connect collective-state verification with temporal-mode analysis of the emitted radiation, offering access to collective coherence with reduced reliance on qubit-resolved correlation measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a matched-mode witnessing protocol that verifies singly excited collective states in a mirror-terminated waveguide QED system by analyzing the temporal mode of the emitted single photon.
AI.motivation: Verifying many-body collective states typically requires qubit-resolved correlation measurements, which are demanding. The authors seek a route to state verification using the common waveguide output instead.
AI.method: The amplitudes and relative phases of the initial collective excitation are encoded in the temporal mode of the emitted single-photon wavepacket. The authors identify the emission mode matching a chosen target state and use an auxiliary virtual-cavity representation to evaluate the quantum state of this selected output mode via a Wigner function.
AI.result: For a matched initial state, the selected mode contains the emitted single photon, whose Wigner function shows a pronounced non-classical negative dip acting as a fingerprint of the target many-body state. With the reference mode fixed, different initial configurations yield different photon occupations and phase-space distributions, confirming state selectivity.
AI.conclusion: The work links collective-state verification to temporal-mode analysis of emitted radiation, enabling access to collective coherence with reduced reliance on qubit-resolved correlation measurements.

title: Time-invariant negativity and persistent bound entanglement in a cyclic two-qutrit family
summary: We study the entanglement dynamics of two qutrits under collective dephasing for a family of states obtained by mixing a maximally entangled state that lives in the decoherence-free subspace with three nonstationary two-term states sharing a common amplitude ratio $r$. We obtain exact PPT and separability regions along the whole trajectory, a specialization of known results on cyclic sign invariant states, and we supply explicit certificates: a finite product decomposition, three fixed positive-map witnesses, and a closed realignment formula that detects every PPT-entangled state, so that no state is left undecided. The negativity is computed in closed form. It shows that the entanglement is time-invariant, positive and constant from the initial time although the state changes, exactly when the weight of the maximally entangled state exceeds the threshold $U_r=r/(1+r+r^2)$. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of time-invariant entanglement for qutrit--qutrit systems under collective dephasing. For smaller weights the entanglement decays and vanishes at a finite time: the state either becomes separable (entanglement sudden death) or, for $r\neq1$ in an intermediate range, loses distillability suddenly and remains bound entangled at all later times. Every state with negative partial transpose is one-copy distillable by a fixed local projection. The same trajectories arise from the global dephasing map and from a correlated local random-unitary semigroup, although the two channels differ on product inputs. Exact rational benchmarks and embeddings of the Horodecki and Ha--Kye--Park families are provided.

AI.tldr: Two qutrits under collective dephasing show time-invariant entanglement when the DFS maximally entangled weight exceeds U_r=r/(1+r+r^2); otherwise entanglement decays, ending in separability (ESD) or sudden loss of distillability to bound entanglement.
AI.motivation: To characterize the entanglement dynamics of qutrit–qutrit (3⊗3) systems under collective dephasing, an open question since prior work mostly addresses qubits, and to provide a fully decided (no undecided states) map of PPT/separability regions along the whole trajectory.
AI.method: Consider a family of states formed by mixing a maximally entangled state in the decoherence-free subspace with three nonstationary two-term states sharing a common amplitude ratio r. Derive exact PPT and separability regions (specializing cyclic sign-invariant state results), and construct explicit certificates: finite product decomposition, three fixed positive-map witnesses, and a closed realignment formula detecting every PPT-entangled state. Compute negativity in closed form; show trajectories coincide for the global dephasing map and a correlated local random-unitary semigroup.
AI.result: Negativity shows entanglement is time-invariant, positive and constant from t=0 exactly when the maximally entangled weight exceeds threshold U_r=r/(1+r+r^2) — the first demonstration of time-invariant qutrit–qutrit entanglement under collective dephasing. Below threshold, entanglement decays and vanishes at finite time: either separability (entanglement sudden death) or, for r≠1 in an intermediate range, sudden loss of distillability with bound entanglement thereafter. Every negative-partial-transpose state is one-copy distillable via a fixed local projection. Exact rational benchmarks and embeddings of Horodecki and Ha–Kye–Park families are given.
AI.conclusion: Collective dephasing yields a sharp weight threshold separating permanent entanglement from decay, with either ESD or bound entanglement as the asymptotic fate; the results provide a complete, certifiable classification plus benchmark states, and extend time-invariant entanglement and ESD phenomena to qutrit systems.

title: On Random Purifications of Isometries and Channels
summary:
Acorn tricks turn weak quantum resources into stronger "randomized" ones. A recent example is the random purification channel, which turns $t$ copies of a mixed state into $t$ copies of a random purification. We ask whether analogous techniques can turn queries to an isometry into queries to a random unitary completion, or queries to a quantum channel into queries to a random isometry dilation.
  For an isometry from dimension $N$ to dimension $M$, we give an efficient, stateful simulator for $T$ sequential, forward queries to a fixed Haar random unitary completion. It uses at most one forward isometry query per simulated call, with total trace-distance error $O(T\sqrt{N/(M-T)})$. This lifts isometry query lower bounds to arbitrary unitary completions, and copy complexity lower bounds to forward access to state preparation unitaries, with dimension-dependent loss that can be made arbitrarily small for most applications.
  Conversely, we construct two distributions on quantum channels distinguishable exactly with two queries to an arbitrary dilation, but requiring exponentially many channel queries for nonnegligible advantage. This rules out efficient simulation of random channel dilations. Our technique also shows that approximating the quantum switch to any constant error below $1/2$ requires exponentially many channel queries, even for identical channels, giving an exponential query advantage for indefinite causal order and improving on Bavaresco et al. (2025).
  Finally, we show how to "decontrol" controlled forward access to an isometry: any algorithm making controlled queries to $φV$ for a random phase $φ$ can be transformed into one using the same number of uncontrolled forward queries to $V$, generalizing the analogous result for unitaries.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether "acorn tricks" (turning weak quantum resources into stronger randomized ones) extend from state purification to isometries and channels: it gives an efficient stateful simulator of a Haar-random unitary completion of an isometry, proves random channel dilations cannot be efficiently simulated, and shows how to decontrol controlled isometry access.
AI.motivation: Acorn tricks have been shown to turn t copies of a mixed state into t copies of a random purification. The authors ask whether analogous techniques can convert queries to an isometry into queries to a random unitary completion, or queries to a quantum channel into queries to a random isometry dilation—potentially lifting existing lower bounds (isometry queries, copy complexity) to more general settings.
AI.method: For an isometry from dimension N to M, construct an efficient stateful simulator for T sequential forward queries to a fixed Haar-random unitary completion, using at most one forward isometry query per simulated call, with total trace-distance error O(T·sqrt(N/(M−T))). Conversely, construct two channel distributions distinguishable with two dilation queries but requiring exponentially many channel queries for nonnegligible advantage. Also apply the technique to the quantum switch and to decontrolling controlled forward access to an isometry (φV with random phase φ).
AI.result: The simulator achieves total trace-distance error O(T·sqrt(N/(M−T))) with one isometry query per call, lifting isometry query lower bounds to arbitrary unitary completions and copy-complexity lower bounds to forward access to state-preparation unitaries (with dimension-dependent loss that is negligible for most applications). The dilation result rules out efficient simulation of random channel dilations. Approximating the quantum switch to any constant error below 1/2 requires exponentially many channel queries, even for identical channels, giving an exponential query advantage for indefinite causal order and improving on Bavaresco et al. (2025). Decontroling shows any algorithm using controlled queries to φV (random phase φ) can be transformed into one with the same number of uncontrolled forward queries to V.
AI.conclusion: Acorn-style techniques do lift isometry queries to random unitary completions (efficient simulation) but provably do NOT extend to random channel dilations (exponentially many channel queries required), yielding an exponential separation for indefinite causal order and a decontrol theorem for isometries generalizing the unitary case.

title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.

AI.tldr: SQMM is a memory-coupled quantum implicit neural representation in which sequential hybrid data-reuploading bands share a coherent quantum memory register; the authors prove the memory forms an operator-valued Fourier series whose support lies in the Minkowski sum of initial memory and local band spectra, and use this to design a spectral memory alignment loss that improves audio and image reconstruction over compact QINR and INR baselines.
AI.motivation: INR performance depends critically on spectral capacity allocation, yet most Quantum INR architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks, preventing later blocks from building on earlier spectral computation. The paper aims to introduce coupling across spectral components so that capacity is allocated more effectively.
AI.method: The Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM) couples sequential hybrid data-reuploading layers (bands) through a shared coherent quantum memory register: each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back. The authors prove that when read and write layers are input independent, the memory state is an operator-valued Fourier series with support contained in the Minkowski sum of initial memory spectrum and local band spectra, with no new primitive frequencies created. This motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages the memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed model prefix.
AI.result: Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.
AI.conclusion: Coupling spectral components through coherent quantum memory yields a principled, spectrally interpretable QINR design whose theoretical frequency-support characterization translates into an effective training objective and better reconstruction performance than compact QINR and INR baselines.

title: Adaptive Self-Optimization of Polarization Efficiency for Low-Power NV Center Thermometers Based on PAS-Q
summary: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have attracted considerable attention for micro- and nanoscale thermometry owing to their high precision and spatial resolution. However, achieving sufficient electron spin polarization and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) typically requires high-power or long-duration laser excitation, which introduces heating and degrades measurement accuracy and stability. To address this trade-off, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach is proposed to optimize spin polarization under low-heating constraints. First, a physical model integrating five-level optical pumping rates and NV spin polarization dynamics is established. A temperature-rise constraint model is then developed based on pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance (P-ODMR) measurements under varying laser powers and pulse widths in an external magnetic field. Subsequently, a Progressive Action-Space Q-learning (PAS-Q) algorithm is employed to explore the parameter space and identify optimal laser power and pulse-width combinations. The agent is trained through numerical simulations and the resulting strategy is implemented in a hardware system. Experimental results demonstrate a 44% reduction in laser-induced heating, a 33% increase in spin polarization rate based on T1 relaxation analysis, and a 71% reduction in optimization time compared with traditional methods. This approach enables efficient spin polarization with reduced laser heating and improved optimization efficiency, and may be extended to other heat-sensitive quantum spin sensors, including silicon-vacancy centers in diamond and divacancy defects in silicon carbide.

AI.tldr: An RL-based method (Progressive Action-Space Q-learning, PAS-Q) optimizes laser power and pulse width for NV-center spin polarization under low-heating constraints, achieving 44% less heating, 33% higher polarization rate, and 71% faster optimization than traditional methods.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity NV-center thermometry needs strong spin polarization and high SNR, but conventional high-power or long-duration laser excitation causes heating that degrades measurement accuracy and stability, creating a polarization-versus-heating trade-off that must be resolved.
AI.method: A five-level optical pumping and NV spin-polarization dynamics model is built, combined with a temperature-rise constraint model derived from pulsed ODMR (P-ODMR) measurements across laser powers and pulse widths under an external magnetic field. A Progressive Action-Space Q-learning (PAS-Q) agent explores the parameter space to find optimal power/pulse-width pairs; it is trained in simulation and deployed on hardware.
AI.result: Compared with traditional methods: 44% reduction in laser-induced heating, 33% increase in spin polarization rate (per T1 relaxation analysis), and 71% reduction in optimization time.
AI.conclusion: The approach achieves efficient spin polarization with reduced laser heating and faster optimization, and is extensible to other heat-sensitive quantum spin sensors such as SiV centers in diamond and divacancy defects in SiC.

title: Cooperative Suppression of Two-Particle Excitation by Kerr Nonlinearity and Cavity Loss ion a Driven Holstein-Tavis-Cumming System
summary: We apply the numerically accurate multiple Davydov Ansatz (multi-$\rm D_2$) method to investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of an open molecular cavity system using an extended driven-dissipative Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model incorporating Kerr nonlinearity. Our results reveal that the synergy between Kerr nonlinearity and exciton-phonon coupling induces an anharmonic level structure, imposing a stringent energy penalty that isolates the one-excitation manifold. This establishes a robust single-excitation-dominated regime that dynamically manifests photon blockade, characterized by suppression of the pure two-photon state and isolation of the one-excitation manifold. While strong coherent driving induces power broadening that overcomes the nonlinear barrier and opens multiphoton channels, cavity dissipation counteracts this process by acting as a highly selective manifold filter. By preferentially depleting fragile multi-photon states while sheltering single excitations within dissipation-free dark states, the cavity mode decay rate actively cooperates with Kerr nonlinearity to restore and reinforce the photon blockade effect. These findings elucidate the intricate interplay among nonlinearity, driving, and dissipation, offering a theoretical blueprint for engineering robust single-photon sources in open molecular cavity platforms.

AI.tldr: The authors use the multiple Davydov Ansatz to simulate an extended driven-dissipative Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model with Kerr nonlinearity, showing that Kerr nonlinearity plus exciton-phonon coupling induces photon blockade, which coherent driving weakens but cavity dissipation restores by filtering out multiphoton states.
AI.motivation: To understand the intricate interplay among Kerr nonlinearity, coherent driving, and cavity dissipation in open molecular cavity systems, and to provide a theoretical basis for engineering robust single-photon sources.
AI.method: Numerically accurate multiple Davydov Ansatz (multi-D2) applied to nonequilibrium dynamics of an extended driven-dissipative Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model incorporating Kerr nonlinearity.
AI.result: Kerr nonlinearity combined with exciton-phonon coupling produces an anharmonic level structure that energetically isolates the one-excitation manifold, yielding photon blockade with suppressed pure two-photon states. Strong coherent driving causes power broadening that overcomes the nonlinear barrier and opens multiphoton channels. Cavity dissipation counteracts this: it preferentially depletes fragile multiphoton states while protecting single excitations in dissipation-free dark states, reinforcing photon blockade.
AI.conclusion: Cavity mode decay actively cooperates with Kerr nonlinearity to restore and reinforce photon blockade, clarifying the nonlinearity-driving-dissipation interplay and offering a blueprint for robust single-photon sources in open molecular cavity platforms.

title: Breakdown of Linearized Dispersion in Waveguide QED
summary: Exploring interactions between quantum emitters and guided photons, waveguide quantum electrodynamics (wQED) offers a versatile platform for quantum simulation and quantum interconnect. To simplify the quantized light-matter interactions, a linearized dispersion approximation (LDA) was widely used in wQED under the conditions of weak coupling and narrow photonic bandwidth. However, a growing number of strong-coupling wQED experiments have called the validity of LDA into question. Here, by investigating giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, we propose a principle to judge the validity of LDA. We find that the decoherence of the atoms exhibits rich dynamical behaviors determined by different numbers of bound states in and out of the continuum (BICs and BOCs) formed in the energy spectrum of the total atom-photon system. Based on this, we show that despite the LDA can partially preserve some of BICs, it completely erases BOCs. This causes the dominant role of LDA in the atomic dynamics to break down. Providing a physical insight into the validity of LDA, our results lay a firm foundation for exploring fundamental physics and its application frontier in strong-coupling wQED platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a principle to judge the validity of the linearized dispersion approximation (LDA) in waveguide QED by studying giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, showing that LDA preserves some bound states in the continuum (BICs) but erases bound states out of the continuum (BOCs), causing the breakdown of LDA's dominant role in atomic dynamics under strong coupling.
AI.motivation: The linearized dispersion approximation (LDA) has been widely used in waveguide QED to simplify quantized light-matter interactions, justified under weak coupling and narrow photonic bandwidth. However, the rise of strong-coupling wQED experiments has called LDA's validity into question, creating a need for a clear criterion to assess when LDA remains reliable.
AI.method: The authors investigate giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, analyzing the energy spectrum of the total atom-photon system and identifying the bound states in the continuum (BICs) and bound states out of the continuum (BOCs). They examine how atomic decoherence dynamics are governed by the number of these bound states, and compare full dispersion results with those obtained under LDA to evaluate its validity.
AI.result: The atomic decoherence exhibits rich dynamical behaviors determined by the different numbers of BICs and BOCs formed in the total atom-photon spectrum. Comparison shows that the LDA can partially preserve some BICs but completely erases BOCs, which causes the LDA to lose its dominant role in describing atomic dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a physical principle for judging the validity of LDA, offering physical insight into its breakdown in the strong-coupling regime and laying a firm foundation for exploring fundamental physics and application frontiers in strong-coupling wQED platforms.

title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit
summary: Quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure hold the potential for computational advantage but are inherently limited by the linear scaling of qubit requirements with respect to system size. Quantum Density Functional Theory (Q-DFT) addresses this constraint by reformulating the interacting many-body problem in terms of a non-interacting Kohn--Sham reference system. Here, we present and experimentally validate a Q-DFT algorithm that requires only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2(N))$ qubits to simulate a system of $N$ orbitals, thereby reducing resource overhead. More precisely, we solve the Kohn--Sham problem for the lithium hydride (LiH) molecule using the ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver paradigm that minimizes the energy of the system in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. To execute this task, we encode the problem with qubits on a quantum photonic platform, utilizing an architecture that combines a deterministic quantum dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit. By evaluating the molecular ground- and first excited-state properties, this work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents and experimentally validates a quantum DFT algorithm that simulates N orbitals using only O(log2(N)) qubits, demonstrated by solving the Kohn-Sham problem for LiH on a photonic platform combining a quantum-dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated circuit.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure suffer from qubit requirements scaling linearly with system size, limiting scalability. Reformulating the interacting many-body problem as a non-interacting Kohn-Sham reference system (Q-DFT) promises to reduce this overhead.
AI.method: A Q-DFT algorithm requiring O(log2(N)) qubits for N orbitals is proposed. The Kohn-Sham problem for LiH is solved using an ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) that minimizes energy in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. The problem is encoded on qubits and executed on a quantum photonic platform using a deterministic quantum-dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit.
AI.result: Successful experimental evaluation of the molecular ground- and first-excited-state properties of LiH, validating the qubit-efficient Q-DFT approach on reconfigurable photonic hardware.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.

title: Temporal stretching of single-photon pulses by intra-cavity frequency conversion
summary: Spectral bandwidth and frequency mismatch between quantum light emitters and quantum components is a common problem in the realization of hybrid quantum information networks. Here we propose a simultaneous solution to both of these problems by using a free-space cavity with an embedded nonlinear crystal that, through frequency conversion, facilitates perfect coupling into a cavity mode. The slow leakage of the cavity effectively stretches the photon pulse, resulting in a much longer photon pulse at a different wavelength. We show that the amount of stretching is strictly limited by the finesse and length of the cavity. Including realistic internal losses in the cavity, we show that it is possible to stretch a photon by at least two orders of magnitude with high efficiency. The proposed setup can thus constitute a valuable addition to the toolbox of quantum information technologies.

AI.tldr: A free-space cavity embedding a nonlinear crystal enables simultaneous spectral-bandwidth matching and frequency conversion, allowing photon pulses to be stretched by at least two orders of magnitude with high efficiency even under realistic internal cavity losses.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum information networks require interfacing quantum light emitters with quantum components, but these suffer from spectral bandwidth mismatch and frequency mismatch. The paper seeks a joint solution to both problems simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors propose a free-space cavity containing an embedded nonlinear crystal. Frequency conversion inside the cavity enables perfect coupling into a cavity mode, while the cavity's slow leakage stretches the photon pulse to a much longer duration at a different wavelength. They derive a strict bound on the achievable stretching set by the cavity finesse and length, and analyze performance including realistic internal losses.
AI.result: The stretching factor is strictly limited by cavity finesse and length. With realistic internal losses included, the scheme can stretch a photon by at least two orders of magnitude (≥100×) while maintaining high efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed setup addresses bandwidth mismatch and frequency mismatch simultaneously, and constitutes a valuable addition to the toolbox of quantum information technologies such as hybrid quantum network interfacing.

title: Mitigating small gaps in quantum annealing through recursive $XX-$catalyst construction
summary: The introduction of $XX-$interactions, typically in the form of an additional catalyst Hamiltonian, has shown promise as a tool for gap enhancement in quantum annealing, allowing the algorithm to obtain optimal solutions with shorter run-times. However, the optimal placements of these couplings within the problem graph has been found to be highly setting-dependent. In this work, we propose an iterative catalyst-construction protocol for the removal of a common quantum annealing bottleneck known as perturbative crossings. The method utilises the measurements returned by successive annealing runs to effectively steer the algorithm away from the local optima in which it becomes trapped. First, we motivate a framework for $XX-$term selection based on perturbation theory and establish its effectiveness at removing perturbative crossings on scalable toy instances with up to $39$ spins, demonstrating a consistent performance both with increasing system size and number of local optima. We then simulate the recursive catalyst-construction method on a test set of $18-$spin maximum-weight independent set problems that are generated to produce annealing spectra with multiple perturbative crossings. We find that the protocol significantly outperforms both catalyst-free annealing and annealing with catalysts containing randomly selected $XX-$terms.

AI.tldr: A paper proposing an iterative, measurement-driven construction of XX-catalyst Hamiltonians that targets and removes perturbative crossings in quantum annealing, outperforming catalyst-free and random-catalyst annealing.
AI.motivation: XX-interactions can enhance the minimum gap in quantum annealing, but the optimal placement of these couplings within the problem graph is highly setting-dependent, and no principled selection rule exists. The work aims to address a common bottleneck—perturbative crossings—with a systematic catalyst-construction protocol.
AI.method: A perturbation-theory-based framework for selecting XX-terms is first motivated to suppress perturbative crossings. Building on this, an iterative catalyst-construction protocol is proposed in which the measurement outcomes of successive annealing runs are used to steer the algorithm away from the local optima in which it becomes trapped, adding catalysts recursively.
AI.result: On scalable toy instances with up to 39 spins, the perturbative-crossing removal is effective and consistent as system size and number of local optima increase. On a test set of 18-spin maximum-weight independent set problems engineered to exhibit multiple perturbative crossings, the recursive protocol significantly outperforms both catalyst-free annealing and annealing with randomly selected XX-term catalysts.
AI.conclusion: Measurement-guided, perturbation-theory-motivated iterative XX-catalyst construction is an effective and scalable strategy for removing perturbative crossings and improving quantum annealing performance over random catalyst placement.

title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times
summary: Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.

AI.tldr: The authors show that the same Kerr nonlinearity that confines Kerr-cat qubit states can also autonomously cool intra-well excitations, extending bit-flip times to 450 s (five orders of magnitude beyond prior work) while preserving fast Z gates and low-error single-shot readout.
AI.motivation: Noise-biased cat qubits suppress bit flips exponentially with photon number, but in Kerr-cat qubits excitations cause interwell switching that caps bit-flip lifetimes at millisecond scales, limiting their practical hardware efficiency.
AI.method: Resonate an intra-well transition with a lossy readout mode so that the confinement-generating nonlinear interaction transfers excitations out of the qubit to be dissipated, verified via spectroscopy and relaxation measurements; additionally characterize Z-gate performance and single-shot readout at operating points with long bit-flip times.
AI.result: Bit-flip times follow the predicted exponential scaling with photon number, reaching 450 s; phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss; fast Z gates show no measurable degradation of bit-flip protection; single-shot readout achieves bit-flip probability below 1e-6 per measurement.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous cooling provides minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, requiring no additional cooling drives or circuit elements.

title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics
summary: Neural networks that predict chaotic dynamics can reproduce short trajectories while misrepresenting statistics over long times. Quantum priors represent selected dynamical statistics through quantum generative models and provide statistical constraints for classical neural networks. Training a separate prior for each value of a system parameter, such as the Reynolds number, does not explicitly model how these statistics vary with that parameter. We learn a conditional quantum prior that approximates selected statistics of an invariant measure at unseen parameter values within the training range, without retraining. For Lorenz-63, the prior reduces mean Jensen-Shannon divergence by 56.9% relative to a classical multilayer perceptron with a comparable number of weights across 96 unseen parameter values. Across 101 values of the same parameter, the shared prior uses 84.7% fewer trainable weights than would be required by a separate quantum neural network at each value. We then use the learned prior to regularize classical neural networks, encouraging their autoregressive rollouts to better reproduce long-term statistics. For Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number $Re=1000$, prior regularization reduces forecast mean squared error by 66.0% over 318 steps relative to the classical baseline without prior regularization. We also implement a photonic quantum prior for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, achieving a mean Jensen-Shannon divergence of $4.58\times10^{-3}$ for Lorenz-63 and $2.59\times10^{-3}$ for Kolmogorov flow at unseen parameter values.

AI.tldr: A single conditional quantum prior models how invariant-measure statistics vary with a system parameter, and it regularizes classical networks for chaotic forecasting.
AI.motivation: Neural networks trained to predict chaotic dynamics fit short trajectories well but misrepresent long-time statistics; existing quantum priors must be trained separately per parameter value and thus fail to capture how statistics vary with that parameter.
AI.method: Learn a conditional quantum generative prior over selected statistics of the invariant measure, for a parameter axis such as Reynolds number, so it generalizes to unseen values within the training range without retraining. The prior is then used to regularize classical autoregressive neural networks.
AI.result: Lorenz-63: 56.9% lower mean Jensen-Shannon divergence than a comparable-size classical MLP across 96 unseen parameter values; 84.7% fewer trainable weights than one quantum neural network per value over 101 values. Kolmogorov flow (Re=1000): prior regularization cuts forecast MSE by 66.0% over 318 steps versus the unregularized baseline. A photonic NISQ prior reaches mean JS divergence of 4.58e-3 (Lorenz-63) and 2.59e-3 (Kolmogorov flow) at unseen parameter values.
AI.conclusion: A single shared conditional quantum prior both generalizes statistical knowledge across system parameters and effectively regularizes classical forecasting models toward correct long-term statistics, with a NISQ-photonic implementation demonstrated.

title: Quantum sensing of a weak drive signal in cascaded quantum van der Pol oscillators
summary: We have constructed a quantum sensing system composed of two quantum van der Pol (vdP) oscillators. Coherent and dissipative couplings are combined to establish a generic nonreciprocal coupling between the two vdP subsystems. A weak driving signal to be measured is applied to an oscillator (probe system) and then transferred via non-reciprocal coupling to another oscillator (measurement system) that is easier to measure. This allows for the acquisition of information about the driving strength of the signal being measured. For the classic cascaded dual vdP oscillators, complete non-reciprocal coupling yields a much higher susceptibility than a single classical vdP oscillator alone. For the quantum vdP system, the sensitivity generally does not diverge at the zero driving force point. When only dissipative coupling and two-particle loss are present, the system will have a dark mode at the zero driving force point, which enables the measurement precision to ultimately reach the Heisenberg limit in the time domain. Enhancing incoherent driving can effectively resist dissipation and thereby improve measurement precision. Moreover, in the strong incoherent driving regime, the improvement factor of non-reciprocal coupling over reciprocal coupling in terms of measurement precision tends to infinity as the two-particle loss rate of the measurement system approaches zero.

AI.tldr: Two nonreciprocally coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators form a sensing setup where a weak signal is transferred from a probe to a measurement oscillator; tailored dissipative coupling with two-particle loss yields a dark mode enabling Heisenberg-limited precision.
AI.motivation: To improve measurement sensitivity of weak driving signals by exploiting nonreciprocal coupling and quantum features of van der Pol oscillators (a probe-to-measurement transfer architecture, analogous to cascaded systems).
AI.method: Construct a quantum sensing system of two quantum vdP oscillators connected by a generic nonreciprocal coupling combining coherent and dissipative couplings. A weak signal drives the probe oscillator and is transferred to the measurement oscillator. Susceptibility/measurement precision are analyzed for classical cascaded dual vdP and quantum vdP cases, including dissipative coupling with two-particle loss, incoherent driving strength, and rate dependence.
AI.result: Classical cascaded dual vdP oscillators with complete nonreciprocal coupling show much higher susceptibility than a single oscillator. For quantum vdP, sensitivity generally does not diverge at zero driving force; with only dissipative coupling and two-particle loss a dark mode appears at zero driving, enabling precision reaching the Heisenberg limit in the time domain. Stronger incoherent driving resists dissipation and improves precision; in the strong incoherent driving regime the nonreciprocal-over-reciprocal precision enhancement factor diverges as the measurement oscillator's two-particle loss rate approaches zero.
AI.conclusion: Nonreciprocal coupling of quantum vdP oscillators, combined with dissipative coupling, two-particle loss, and strong incoherent driving, provides an effective route to enhanced, Heisenberg-limited weak-signal sensing, with the advantage over reciprocal coupling becoming arbitrarily large in the appropriate limits.

title: Fast verification of fault tolerant magic state preparation circuits with the CNOT + T gate set
summary: Magic state preparation is often among the most expensive operations in a fault tolerant quantum computation. One obstacle to coming up with better magic state preparation circuits lies in verifying their fault tolerance properties, as it is difficult to verify either by hand or in software that a very large number of combinations of faults do not give rise to high-weight or logical errors, especially in a non-Clifford circuit. In this work, we propose the use of the CNOT + T gate set to fault-tolerantly prepare a large class of magic states. We consider the propagation of Pauli faults within CNOT + T circuits and derive properties similar to those of Pauli faults within Clifford circuits, with a view to verifying fault tolerance as efficiently as possible. We present Comb, a library that can verify the fault tolerance of CNOT + T magic state preparation circuits, and demonstrate its use in verifying the fault tolerance of distance three and distance five magic state preparation circuits in minutes on a laptop. We present a distance five magic state preparation circuit that was discovered using Comb. As an independent confirmation of Comb's correctness we compare its findings to circuit-level noisy simulations for several magic state preparation circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CNOT+T magic state preparation circuits, derives Pauli-fault propagation properties analogous to Clifford circuits, and introduces Comb, a tool verifying fault tolerance of such circuits (d=3 and d=5) in minutes, validated against noisy simulations.
AI.motivation: Magic state preparation is among the most expensive operations in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Designing better preparation circuits is hindered by the difficulty of verifying fault tolerance: it is hard, by hand or by software, to confirm that an enormous number of fault combinations do not produce high-weight or logical errors, particularly in non-Clifford circuits.
AI.method: The authors use the CNOT+T gate set to fault-tolerantly prepare a broad class of magic states. They analyze the propagation of Pauli faults through CNOT+T circuits and derive properties analogous to those of Pauli faults in Clifford circuits, enabling efficient fault-tolerance verification. They implement this as Comb, a library for verifying fault tolerance of CNOT+T magic state preparation circuits, and independently validate it against circuit-level noisy simulations.
AI.result: Comb verifies fault tolerance of distance-three and distance-five magic state preparation circuits within minutes on a laptop. Using Comb, the authors discover a distance-five magic state preparation circuit. Independent comparison of Comb's findings with circuit-level noisy simulations across several circuits confirms its correctness.
AI.conclusion: Pauli-fault propagation in CNOT+T circuits has tractable structure analogous to Clifford circuits, making fault-tolerance verification practical. Comb enables efficient design and verification of magic state preparation circuits and supports discovery of new distance-five circuits.

title: Transferable Lindblad Variational Ansatz for Accelerated Steady-State Preparation
summary: Open quantum systems naturally relax toward steady states that underpin diverse nonequilibrium phenomena and quantum technologies. We independently control the coherent and dissipative constituents of a Lindblad generator to construct a variational product formula, termed the Lindblad variational ansatz (LVA), that accelerates steady-state preparation over natural relaxation through an optimized preparation path. The protocol consists of small-system learning, continuation to greater depth, and transfer to larger systems, followed when needed by reference-free post-training on quantum simulators. We demonstrate LVA in a bulk-dissipative Ising chain and a boundary-driven Heisenberg chain, where transferred protocols achieve matched preparation accuracies with fewer generator blocks than time-optimized first- and second-order Trotter formulas. The acceleration arises from coordinated endpoint preparation: earlier controls shape the dissipative-mode amplitudes so that the final dissipative step brings multiple components simultaneously close to their target values. Our results suggest a route to open-system quantum simulation that combines classical training on small systems with deployment and optional refinement on larger quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Lindblad variational ansatz (LVA), a variational product formula that independently controls the coherent and dissipative parts of a Lindblad generator to accelerate steady-state preparation of open quantum systems beyond natural relaxation.
AI.motivation: Open quantum systems relax toward steady states underpinning nonequilibrium phenomena and quantum technologies, but natural relaxation is slow. The authors aim to speed up steady-state preparation by optimizing the preparation path rather than relying on free relaxation.
AI.method: They independently control coherent and dissipative constituents of a Lindblad generator to build a variational product formula (LVA). The protocol comprises small-system learning, continuation to greater depth, and transfer to larger systems, optionally followed by reference-free post-training on quantum simulators.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a bulk-dissipative Ising chain and a boundary-driven Heisenberg chain, transferred LVA protocols reach matched preparation accuracy using fewer generator blocks than time-optimized first- and second-order Trotter formulas. The speedup stems from coordinated endpoint preparation: earlier controls shape dissipative-mode amplitudes so the final dissipative step brings multiple components near their targets simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest a route to open-system quantum simulation that couples classical training on small systems with deployment and optional refinement on larger quantum devices.

title: Substantially Improved Rate and Distance for Addressable Transversal Phase Gates
summary: An important ingredient in fault-tolerant quantum computation is asymptotically good codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford gates. Existing constructions, however, provide only small explicit guarantees for rate and relative distance. Here, we substantially improve these guarantees for fully addressable transversal phase gates at every fixed level $h\ge3$ of the Clifford hierarchy, using a cyclic encoding beyond the binary CSS framework. The encoding separates logical phase control from the joint design of rate and distance, enabling two constructions with different computational costs. A deterministic polynomial-time algebraic-geometric construction gives a common asymptotic lower bound of $52/(675h)$ on both quantities. A counting argument gives an exponential-time construction with exact verification, improving this bound by a factor of approximately $2.86$. We further establish a universal upper bound for codes supporting fully addressable transversal single-qubit phase gates. Within our cyclic encoding framework, we obtain a stronger upper bound that is approximately $1.28$ times the lower bound achieved by our exponential-time construction. As concrete examples, we construct codes with $48$ and $90$ physical qubits supporting fully addressable transversal $T$ gates. These results narrow the gap between achievable code parameters and addressability bounds, providing quantitative targets for further improvements in efficient code constructions.

AI.tldr: Asymptotically good codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford gates are improved in rate and relative distance for all fixed levels h≥3 of the Clifford hierarchy, using a cyclic encoding beyond binary CSS.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation needs asymptotically good codes supporting fully addressable transversal non-Clifford gates, but existing constructions give only small explicit guarantees on rate and relative distance.
AI.method: A cyclic encoding outside the binary CSS framework separates logical phase control from the joint rate–distance design, yielding two constructions: a deterministic polynomial-time algebraic-geometric construction, and a counting argument giving an exponential-time construction with exact verification. Universal upper bounds for codes supporting fully addressable transversal single-qubit phase gates are also derived, with a stronger bound within the cyclic encoding framework. Concrete 48- and 90-qubit codes with fully addressable transversal T gates are constructed.
AI.result: The algebraic-geometric construction achieves a common asymptotic lower bound of 52/(675h) on both rate and relative distance; the exponential-time construction improves this by about a factor of 2.86. The stronger upper bound within the cyclic framework is about 1.28× the exponential-time lower bound.
AI.conclusion: The results narrow the gap between achievable code parameters and addressability bounds, providing quantitative targets for further improvements in efficient code constructions.

title: Synchronization Mpemba Effect
summary: We introduce the synchronization Mpemba effect, in which a less synchronized initial state overtakes a more synchronized one, and demonstrate it in dissipatively coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators. Within a graph-Laplacian framework, we show that for two oscillators, the mechanism is a competition between a slowly decaying collective background and a fast transverse transient, equivalently an exchange between relative-mode displacement and phase-fluctuation errors. The same decomposition extends to networks: the synchronization error splits into transverse Laplacian modes, yielding closed-form crossing times from eigenvalue separations and initial mode weights, and a sufficient screening criterion. With only these eigenvalues entering, the rule is topology independent: crossing times of different networks collapse onto a single spectral-gap line. Thus, quantum many-body dynamics can be designed and controlled at low dimension without constructing the exponentially large Liouvillian, opening a route to quantum synchronization as a resource.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "synchronization Mpemba effect," where a less synchronized initial state overtakes a more synchronized one, and demonstrates it in dissipatively coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators using a graph-Laplacian framework.
AI.motivation: Synchronization is typically expected to improve monotonically from better initial conditions; the authors aim to show a counterintuitive overtaking effect and establish a scalable, low-dimensional means of predicting and controlling quantum many-body synchronization dynamics without constructing the exponentially large Liouvillian.
AI.method: A graph-Laplacian decomposition is used.
