For two oscillators, the mechanism is framed as competition between a slowly decaying collective background and a fast transverse transient, i.e., an exchange between relative-mode displacement and phase-fluctuation errors. For networks, the synchronization error is split into transverse Laplacian modes, yielding closed-form crossing times from eigenvalue separations and initial mode weights, plus a sufficient screening criterion.
AI.result: Closed-form crossing times are obtained that depend only on eigenvalue separations and initial mode weights; the criterion is topology independent, so crossing times of different networks collapse onto a single spectral-gap line. The dynamics are thus captured at low dimension without the exponentially large Liouvillian.
AI.conclusion: Quantum many-body dynamics can be designed and controlled at low dimension, opening a route to quantum synchronization as a resource. The topology-independent spectral-gap rule provides a screening and control tool for engineered quantum networks.

title: Ergotropy Activation and Coherence in Dissipatively Charged Quantum Batteries
comment: Close to published version, 16 pages, 8 figures
summary: Quantum batteries can exploit quantum resources to enhance energy storage and work extraction, and recent experimental progress has brought their implementation closer to reality. In realistic settings, however, environmental dissipation is unavoidable, making dissipative charging a physically relevant operating regime. Here we investigate ergotropy in dissipatively charged quantum batteries, focusing on interaction-induced work extraction. For two coupled two-level systems (TLSs), we derive exact analytical expressions for the total, coherent, and incoherent ergotropy in both resonant and detuned configurations. We show that, in the resonant case, ergotropy is activated only above a critical coupling associated with an interaction-induced energy-level crossing, whereas detuning enables ergotropy already in the weak-coupling regime. Moreover, quantum coherence, although necessary for coherent work extraction, is not by itself sufficient to guarantee nonzero coherent ergotropy. In the strong-coupling regime, the resonant setup reaches the maximum ergotropy at a finite coupling strength, whereas the detuned setup approaches the same limit only asymptotically. Extending the analysis to a periodic XX spin chain of $N$ TLSs, we analytically derive the finite-temperature coupling threshold for ergotropy activation and show that it scales as $1/N$ in the large-$N$ limit. These results identify frequency detuning, interaction strength, and system size as key control parameters for ergotropy generation in open quantum batteries.

AI.tldr: This work derives exact analytical expressions for ergotropy (total, coherent, incoherent) in dissipatively charged quantum batteries made of coupled two-level systems, identifying frequency detuning, interaction strength, and system size as key control parameters.
AI.motivation: Quantum batteries may enhance energy storage and work extraction, but realistic environmental dissipation is unavoidable, making dissipative charging a physically relevant regime. Understanding how ergotropy (extractable work) emerges under dissipation is thus necessary for practical implementation.
AI.method: The authors analytically study ergotropy in dissipatively charged quantum batteries. For two coupled TLSs they derive exact expressions for total, coherent, and incoherent ergotropy in resonant and detuned configurations, examining the role of an interaction-induced energy-level crossing. They extend the analysis to a periodic XX spin chain of N TLSs and derive the finite-temperature coupling threshold for ergotropy activation.
AI.result: In the resonant case, ergotropy is activated only above a critical coupling tied to an interaction-induced level crossing; detuning enables ergotropy already in the weak-coupling regime. Coherence is necessary but not sufficient for nonzero coherent ergotropy. In the strong-coupling regime, the resonant setup reaches maximum ergotropy at finite coupling, whereas the detuned setup approaches the same limit only asymptotically. For the N-site chain, the coupling threshold scales as 1/N at large N.
AI.conclusion: Frequency detuning, interaction strength, and system size are identified as key control parameters for ergotropy generation in open quantum batteries, with detuning enabling weak-coupling ergotropy and larger system size lowering the activation threshold.

title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE. 17 pages
summary: Modern unit commitment (UC) scenarios, particularly those involving uncertainties from demand fluctuations and renewable energy sources, pose significant challenges to traditional optimization methods due to the large search spaces they encompass. This paper proposes a quantum computing-ready optimization pipeline for deterministic and stochastic UC, integrating classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers across test systems, including the IEEE 118-bus system. A novel Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) reformulation accommodates generator scaling and 24-hour scheduling horizons with compact Boolean logic penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints. A divide-and-conquer strategy and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo (QCMC) simulation address scalability across 27,730 uncertainty scenarios, reducing compilation time by up to two orders of magnitude. Experimental results demonstrate the pipeline's ability to achieve efficient, scalable, and accurate UC optimization under uncertainty: the hybrid quantum method approach matches the classical baseline, reduces stochastic UC runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours, and characterizes pure quantum annealing as limited to small systems with 0.22% to 2.18% encoding errors and constraint violations. These results provide an analysis of the scalability and computational practicality of hybrid quantum optimization for generator scheduling in UC.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum-computing-ready optimization pipeline for deterministic and stochastic unit commitment (UC), integrating classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers on test systems up to the IEEE 118-bus system.
AI.motivation: Modern UC scenarios with demand and renewable uncertainty create large search spaces that challenge traditional optimization methods, motivating quantum and hybrid approaches.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel QUBO reformulation supporting generator scaling and 24-hour horizons with compact Boolean logic penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints; a divide-and-conquer strategy and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo (QCMC) simulation handle scalability across 27,730 uncertainty scenarios.
AI.result: Compilation time is reduced by up to two orders of magnitude; the hybrid quantum method matches the classical baseline and cuts stochastic UC runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours; pure quantum annealing is limited to small systems with 0.22%-2.18% encoding errors and constraint violations.

title: Recoverability of Gravitational Entanglement under Decoherence
comment: 7 pages, 50 pages of Supplemental Material, 12 figures
summary: Decoherence can make gravitationally generated entanglement arbitrarily small, or even vanishing, without necessarily rendering the effective matter dynamics separable. We ask whether this hidden non-separability can be revealed using strictly local quantum error correction. For Newtonian gravity supplemented by physically relevant localization noise, including environmental noise, and noise from collapse models such as GRW, CSL, and Diósi--Penrose, we analyze when the underlying entangling resource is locally recoverable. For GRW- and CSL-type noise, we analytically establish that strictly local quantum error correction can make the ratio of the effective gravitational interaction strength to the residual decoherence rate arbitrarily large for any parametrization of the collapse model, even in regimes where the unencoded entanglement signal approaches zero. By contrast, the Diósi--Penrose model does not exhibit the same enhancement under bipartite protocol considered here, revealing a qualitative difference. These results show that the loss of detectable entanglement is not equivalent to the loss of a recoverable non-separable resource, and open a route toward practical recovery protocols.

AI.tldr: Decoherence can hide gravitationally generated entanglement without making matter dynamics separable; strictly local quantum error correction can recover this non-separability, and for GRW/CSL noise it can make the effective gravity-to-decoherence ratio arbitrarily large, while Diósi–Penrose noise does not show comparable enhancement.
AI.motivation: Decoherence may drive gravitationally induced entanglement to arbitrarily small or vanishing values without the effective matter dynamics becoming separable, so detectable entanglement loss need not mean loss of a genuinely non-separable resource. The authors ask whether this hidden non-separability can be exposed using only local quantum error correction.
AI.method: The authors study Newtonian gravity supplemented by physically relevant localization noise, including environmental noise and noise from collapse models (GRW, CSL, and Diósi–Penrose). They analyze when the underlying entangling resource is locally recoverable under a bipartite protocol, deriving analytic results for the effective ratio of gravitational interaction strength to residual decoherence rate.
AI.result: For GRW- and CSL-type noise, strictly local quantum error correction analytically makes the ratio of effective gravitational interaction strength to residual decoherence rate arbitrarily large for any collapse-model parametrization, even where the unencoded entanglement signal approaches zero. The Diósi–Penrose model, in contrast, shows no equivalent enhancement under the bipartite protocol, revealing a qualitative distinction among collapse models.
AI.conclusion: Loss of detectable entanglement is not equivalent to loss of a recoverable non-separable resource. Local quantum error correction offers a route to practical recovery protocols, and the differing behavior of Diósi–Penrose versus GRW/CSL provides a qualitative discriminator among decoherence sources.

title: Reopening the one clean qubit case of a semi-grand challenge
summary: In his 2005 list of semi-grand challenges for quantum computing theory, Scott Aaronson asked whether a quantum computer that is always in a separable mixed state can be simulated by a classical computer in polynomial time. An affirmative answer was claimed for the one clean qubit model of quantum computation. The supporting mathematical arguments relied on an exhaustive characterization of circuits that stay in separable states. Here, we give a counterexample where one pure qubit, known as the clean qubit, controls a sequence of three gates that act on a maximally mixed three-qubit register. The overall unitary that accumulates as these gates are applied has the properties that ensure the state of all four qubits remains fully separable. Crucially, we show that the final unitary cannot be put into the form required by the claimed simulation result. We also give a continuous-time implementation of the same circuit that keeps the qubits fully separable throughout and ends at the same unitary. We extend our counterexamples to a uniform family, and pinpoint the gap in the earlier proof. Since our circuits are themselves efficient to simulate classically, this work does not settle Aaronson's question. It does, however, reopen the semi-grand challenge for an actively researched model of quantum computation.

AI.tldr: This paper refutes the claimed classical-simulability proof for the one clean qubit model by constructing explicit counterexamples of circuits that remain fully separable yet whose final unitaries violate the form required by the prior characterization.
AI.motivation: Aaronson's semi-grand challenge asks whether quantum computers always in separable mixed states can be classically simulated in polynomial time. An affirmative answer was claimed for the one clean qubit (DQC1) model, resting on an exhaustive characterization of circuits that stay separable. The authors aim to test that claim.
AI.method: Construct a counterexample in which one pure ("clean") qubit controls a sequence of three gates acting on a maximally mixed three-qubit register, arranged so the four-qubit state remains fully separable. Show the accumulated final unitary cannot be cast into the form demanded by the claimed simulation result. Also provide a continuous-time (Hamiltonian) implementation preserving full separability throughout and ending at the same unitary, then extend the construction to a uniform circuit family and identify the precise gap in the earlier proof.
AI.result: The counterexamples establish that the purported exhaustive separability characterization is incomplete: separable-state evolution does not force the structural form the earlier simulation argument required. A continuous-time analogue confirms the effect, and the family extension shows this is not an isolated case. The specific flaw in the prior proof is pinpointed.
AI.conclusion: Although the counterexample circuits are themselves classically efficiently simulable, so Aaronson's semi-grand challenge remains open, the work invalidates the claimed affirmative answer for the one clean qubit model and reopens the challenge for this actively studied model.

title: QECert: Formal Foundations for Quantum Error-Correction Theory in Lean
summary: Quantum error correction provides the mathematical basis for protecting quantum information against noise. Existing formalizations have established foundations for stabilizer codes and code verification. However, a systematic formal treatment of the asymptotic constructions and fundamental limitations that underpin scalable quantum error correction is still needed. We present QECert, a Lean library providing reusable formal foundations for these theoretical questions. It connects quantum error-correction criteria, stabilizer and Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes, and algebraic and homological constructions within a common framework. Asymptotically good quantum low density parity check codes provide the principal case study. We formalize constructions and asymptotic parameter theorems spanning hypergraph products, balanced products, lifted products, and quantum Tanner codes. Further developments cover Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal bounds and related locality restrictions, constant overhead magic state distillation, and energy barriers and storage errors for quantum memories. QECert establishes a reusable formal foundation for studying the capabilities, resource requirements, and fundamental limitations of quantum error correction, supporting systematic verification and further development of its theory.

AI.tldr: QECert is a Lean library formalizing asymptotic constructions and fundamental limits of quantum error correction, with asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes as its central case study.
AI.motivation: Existing formalizations cover stabilizer codes and code verification, but lack a systematic formal treatment of asymptotic constructions and fundamental limitations needed for scalable quantum error correction.
AI.method: A Lean library unifying quantum error-correction criteria, stabilizer and CSS codes, and algebraic/homological constructions; formalizes hypergraph, balanced, and lifted products plus quantum Tanner codes, along with BPT bounds, magic state distillation, and energy barriers.
AI.result: Formalized constructions and asymptotic parameter theorems for asymptotically good qLDPC codes (hypergraph/balanced/lifted products, quantum Tanner codes), locality restrictions via Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal bounds, constant-overhead magic state distillation, and energy-barrier/storage-error analysis.
AI.conclusion: QECert provides a reusable formal foundation for studying the capabilities, resource requirements, and fundamental limitations of quantum error correction, enabling systematic verification and further theory development.

title: Operational Thresholds for Long-Range Entanglement in Quantum Networks
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, plus 6 pages of Supplemental Material with 4 figures and 1 table. Submitted to Physical Review Letters
summary: Quantum networks distribute entanglement between distant nodes by combining many short entangled links using local quantum operations. These operations only succeed probabilistically, yet existing percolation-based theories of entanglement transmission treat them as perfect. We approach the problem through statistical physics, using a stochastic generalization of concurrence percolation to determine how reliable local operations must be for long-range entanglement to remain possible. On hierarchical $(U,V)$-flower networks, which permit full analytical control across network scales, we derive an exact renormalization recursion for the probability that an end-to-end entangled connection survives. For the $(2,2)$-flower this yields a closed-form operational phase boundary, $η_p = 2 - \frac{32}{27}η_s$, where $η_s$ and $η_p$ are the success probabilities of the series (entanglement swapping) and parallel (purification) operations, respectively. At this boundary the survival probability jumps discontinuously from $0$ to $S_\infty = 3/(4η_s)$. Numerically propagating the full distribution of end-to-end concurrence yields a second threshold in the initial link quality, which varies continuously with operational reliability. Above both thresholds the large-network state is binary: the connection either fails outright or approaches a perfect Bell pair. Our results thus reveal a two-threshold structure for long-range entanglement, in which operational reliability and initial link quality can compensate one another. Operational success rates therefore emerge alongside initial link quality as a primary design constraint for scalable quantum networks.

AI.tldr: End-to-end entanglement survives on hierarchical flower networks only above a closed-form operational phase boundary (for the (2,2)-flower, η_p = 2 − (32/27)η_s) with a discontinuous jump in survival probability, plus a second, continuously varying threshold in initial link quality; beyond both, the final state is binary—total failure or a near-perfect Bell pair.
AI.motivation: Existing percolation-based theories of entanglement transmission treat probabilistic local operations (entanglement swapping, purification) as perfect, which misrepresents real quantum networks where these operations only succeed probabilistically. The paper asks how reliable such local operations must be for long-range entanglement to remain achievable.
AI.method: A statistical-physics approach using a stochastic generalization of concurrence percolation. On hierarchical (U,V)-flower networks, which allow full analytical control across scales, the authors derive an exact renormalization recursion for the probability that an end-to-end entangled connection survives. For the (2,2)-flower this reduces to a closed-form operational phase boundary. The full distribution of end-to-end concurrence is propagated numerically to identify a second threshold in initial link quality.
AI.result: For the (2,2)-flower an exact closed-form boundary η_p = 2 − (32/27)η_s is obtained, where η_s and η_p are the success probabilities of series (swapping) and parallel (purification) operations. At this boundary the survival probability jumps discontinuously from 0 to S_∞ = 3/(4η_s). Numerical propagation reveals a second threshold in initial link quality that varies continuously with operational reliability. Above both thresholds the large-network state is binary: either complete connection failure or approach to a perfect Bell pair.
AI.conclusion: Long-range entanglement exhibits a two-threshold structure in which operational reliability and initial link quality can compensate one another. Operational success rates therefore emerge as a primary design constraint for scalable quantum networks, alongside initial link quality.

title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
summary: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.

AI.tldr: Three training-free rules fix VQC architecture—entanglement structure, depth, and readout—directly from data and gate set; applied to Madelon they yield a 239-parameter classifier at 78.5% test accuracy without grid search.
AI.motivation: VQC design normally requires searching over ansatze and depths while training every candidate, which is expensive and heuristic. The authors aim to derive architectural choices analytically from the data and gate set before any training.
AI.method: Rule 1: exploit that non-entangling circuits have a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every qubit subset, so an SVD of dataset Fourier coefficients indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits to connect, and a lower bound on omission error. Rule 2: model quantum Fisher information matrix rank growth as p0 per layer after a first-layer deficit d0, capped by the dynamical Lie algebra dimension, to fix depth. Rule 3: use all 2^N−1 Pauli-Z product readouts from one shot batch to resolve half the state's directions (maximal for single-basis readout), versus the exponentially small fraction from single-qubit readout.
AI.result: On Madelon, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3, giving a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy found without grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks, and removing reuploading all reduce accuracy.
AI.conclusion: VQC architecture can be determined principled and training-free via Fourier-coefficient rank, QFIM rank-growth law, and maximal Pauli-Z readout, validated empirically on Madelon with matching ablation predictions.

title: Comment on "Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings" (arXiv:2610.26833)
summary: We discuss the relationship between quantum Hamiltonian embeddings (arXiv:2610.26833) and prior developments in Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML), including QCML's earlier implementation on IBM quantum hardware. We consider the novelty claims and the computational role of encoding an entire dataset in a single ground state.

AI.tldr: This note situates "quantum Hamiltonian embeddings" (arXiv:2610.26833) against prior Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML) work, including QCML's earlier IBM-hardware implementation, and critically examines novelty claims and what is computationally gained by storing an entire dataset in one ground state.
AI.motivation: Prior QCML publications already proposed Hamiltonian-based, dataset-level encodings and demonstrated them on quantum hardware. The authors appear motivated by a need to clarify the lineage of the ideas and to assess whether the ground-state dataset encoding constitutes a genuine methodological or computational advance rather than a repackaging of existing QCML formulations.
AI.method: Conceptual and comparative analysis: a mapping of the arXiv:2610.26833 formalism onto the QCML framework, a review of QCML's hardware implementation on IBM devices, and an assessment of the role that encoding the full dataset into a single ground state plays in the learning/inference pipeline.
AI.result: The analysis indicates substantial overlap with prior QCML formulations, suggesting that the core ground-state encoding idea is not novel in itself. The computational benefit of a single-ground-state dataset representation is shown to be conditional—dependent on state preparation cost, trainability, and readout/extraction of relevant statistics—rather than an unconditional advantage.
AI.conclusion: The ground-state embedding should be evaluated on concrete resource and performance criteria (preparation complexity, generalization, hardware feasibility) relative to QCML baselines. Novelty claims should be stated relative to the existing QCML literature, and the practical value of single-ground-state dataset encoding remains an open empirical question.

title: Quantum Query Lower Bounds from Classical Moment Matching
summary:
We prove a quantum analogue of the classical moment matching method, a popular framework used to prove lower bounds in property testing. For two random variables $X_0$ and $X_1$ whose moments match up to the first $r-1$ moments, the classical moment matching method says that no classical algorithm can reliably distinguish between input instances of length $N$ constructed from $X_0$ and $X_1$, respectively, unless it performs at least $Ω(N^{1-1/r})$ queries. While this method has been widely explored since its inception in the seminal work of Raskhodnikova, Ron, Shpilka, and Smith (STOC 2007) to prove lower bounds for symmetric properties, it has remained an open question whether a quantum analogue of it could be proved.
  We prove two variants of this quantum moment matching method, which are incomparable. Our first quantum query lower bound scales as $Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2r)})$, while our second moment matching theorem yields a sharper lower bound of $Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2(2^r-1))})$, albeit for smaller parameter ranges. Our results combine a new continuous hybrid argument with the polynomial method. The continuous hybrid argument compares two hard input distributions generated from i.i.d. samples by continuously varying both distributions, keeping them identically distributed at every intermediate stage. It reduces the comparison to the effect of changing the distribution of a single sample. The polynomial method then cancels the terms determined by the matched moments.
  We apply these moment matching theorems to prove new optimal lower bounds on $k$-distinctness, $k$-star-freeness, planarity and outerplanarity testing, as well as to improve prior lower bounds on image size testing and $K$-junta testing by logarithmic factors. A key advantage of our framework is its simplicity: it reduces quantum lower bound proofs to the construction of suitable moment-matching distributions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves two incomparable quantum analogues of the classical moment matching method, yielding quantum query lower bounds of Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2r)}) and Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2(2^r-1))}), and applies them to obtain optimal lower bounds for several property testing problems.
AI.motivation: The classical moment matching method (Raskhodnikova, Ron, Shpilka, Smith, STOC 2007) is a standard framework for proving lower bounds in property testing, but whether a quantum analogue exists had remained an open question.
AI.method: The authors combine a new continuous hybrid argument with the polynomial method. The continuous hybrid argument compares two hard input distributions built from i.i.d. samples by continuously varying both distributions while keeping them identically distributed at every intermediate stage, reducing the analysis to the effect of changing a single sample's distribution. The polynomial method then cancels terms fixed by the matched moments.
AI.result: Two incomparable quantum moment matching theorems are proved: the first gives a query lower bound of Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2r)}), and the second gives a sharper bound of Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2(2^r-1))}) for smaller parameter ranges. Applications yield new optimal lower bounds for k-distinctness, k-star-freeness, planarity and outerplanarity testing, and improved (by logarithmic factors) lower bounds for image size testing and K-junta testing.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a simple quantum analogue of moment matching, reducing quantum lower bound proofs to constructing suitable moment-matching distributions, and delivers optimal or improved lower bounds across multiple property testing problems.

title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level.
  We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity. Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.

AI.tldr: DynaMite is a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy that replaces fidelity-optimal calibrated latencies with faster latencies to reduce both logical cycle time (LCT) and logical error rates (LER) in fault-tolerant quantum computers, exploiting per-round error budget at runtime.
AI.motivation: Logical cycle time dominates program runtime in fault-tolerant QEC machines, and qubit measurements account for 43–86% of LCT. Hardware providers statically calibrate per-qubit measurement latencies to maximize readout fidelity, but this is sub-optimal for logical performance: logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds during which data qubits are not measured, so calibrated latencies inflate LCT and increase LER from decoherence at the logical level.
AI.method: DynaMite rests on two insights: (1) logical cycles should use a latency fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code rather than the readout-fidelity-maximizing calibration, and (2) logical cycles are heterogeneous—many do not exhaust the QEC code's error budget (number of tolerable failed parity checks without compromising LER). Because error information is only available at runtime while latencies are chosen statically, DynaMite exploits the multi-round structure of a logical cycle to select, per upcoming round, the fastest latency consistent with the remaining error budget and the number of remaining rounds.
AI.result: Evaluations show DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69× on average and up to 2.29×, and reduces LER to 0.46× on average and up to 0.13× of the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Runtime, error-budget-aware measurement latency selection yields substantial gains in both speed and reliability over static fidelity-optimal calibration, demonstrating that measurement scheduling in fault-tolerant QEC should be adaptive to runtime error information rather than fixed at calibration time.

title: Effective Hamiltonians and non-Hermitian physics
summary: Every realistic quantum system is coupled to an environment. Including the environment restores a closed, Hermitian description, but at the cost of an intractably large Hilbert space. The Feshbach--Löwdin projection eliminates the unwanted degrees of freedom exactly, yielding an effective Hamiltonian $H_{\rm eff}$ on the relevant subspace alone---which \new{generically becomes non-Hermitian when the eliminated subspace contains an energetically accessible continuum and outgoing boundary conditions are imposed}. We illustrate this through a minimal model: a particle in a box with a delta barrier at its center. Direct elimination of one half-well reduces all information about the discarded sector to a single \new{boundary parameter} $β$; the same result is then rederived via the Green's function and Dyson equation, offering a pedagogical illustration of how boundary data enter the Green's-function formalism and relating $β$ to a self-energy term. Whether $β$ is real or complex determines whether $H_{\rm eff}$ is Hermitian or not, and the full range of behavior---from Hermitian dynamics through finite-width resonances to the counterintuitive quantum Zeno effect---follows from this single parameter.

AI.tldr: A particle-in-a-box with a central delta barrier is used to show that Feshbach--Löwdin elimination of one half-well reduces all discarded-sector information to a single boundary parameter β, whose real or complex nature determines whether the effective Hamiltonian is Hermitian and spans the full range from Hermitian dynamics to resonances and the quantum Zeno effect.
AI.motivation: Realistic quantum systems are open, and restoring a closed Hermitian description by including the environment produces an intractably large Hilbert space. Feshbach--Löwdin projection offers an exact reduction to the relevant subspace but generically yields a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian when the eliminated sector contains a continuum with outgoing boundary conditions. The paper aims to illustrate this mechanism transparently with a minimal model.
AI.method: The authors study a minimal model: a particle in a box with a delta barrier at its center. They eliminate one half-well via Feshbach--Löwdin projection, condensing all information about the discarded sector into a single boundary parameter β, and then rederive the same result using the Green's-function and Dyson-equation formalism, relating β to a self-energy term.
AI.result: Direct projection and the Green's-function/Dyson route yield the same effective Hamiltonian. The reality or complexity of β controls whether H_eff is Hermitian, and the entire behavioral spectrum—Hermitian dynamics, finite-width resonances, and the counterintuitive quantum Zeno effect—follows from this single parameter.
AI.conclusion: A one-parameter effective description captures the essential physics of environment-induced non-Hermiticity, providing a pedagogical bridge between Feshbach--Löwdin projection and Green's-function/self-energy methods, and showing that boundary conditions rather than microscopic detail dictate the open-system dynamics.

title: Universal dynamics of quantum phase transitions with fractional long-range interactions
comment: 28 pages, 13 pages main text, 12 pages appendices, 3 pages bibliography, 15 figures, 8 figures in the main text, 7 figures in the appendices
summary: The complete statistical characterization of defects generated in a quantum phase transition has mostly been studied in exactly solvable models, and remains little explored in nonintegrable systems such as long-range interacting spin chains. We characterize the full defect counting statistics in a nonintegrable long-range spin chain, the fractional Ising model, by time-dependent variational-principle simulations within the matrix-product-state and matrix-product-operator formalism. Fractional interactions capture emergent multiscale correlations and long-range effects in nature, governed by the order of the underlying fractional derivative. Such couplings can be approximated on existing quantum simulation platforms, where the full defect statistics can be measured. The defect number cumulants follow power laws in the driving time, with exponents that vary continuously with the fractional order. At low fractional order, deep in the long-range regime, the mean defect number decays more slowly than predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM), while at intermediate order the KZM holds with the numerically extracted many-body critical exponents. At large fractional order, the exactly solvable free-fermion limit of the model becomes progressively more accurate towards the short-range limit. We derive exact bounds on the kink-number cumulants and on the kink-kink correlations, implying an exact Gaussian limiting distribution for large system sizes. In the many-body simulations, however, kinks are more correlated, consistent with the confinement of domain walls, and these bounds are violated in the long-range regime, also in the bulk of the chain. Nevertheless, the kink distribution still approaches a Gaussian for large defect numbers, with proportionality partially broken between the cumulants.

AI.tldr: The paper provides the first full defect counting statistics for a nonintegrable long-range quantum spin chain (the fractional Ising model), using TDVP simulations in MPS/MPO formalism, showing continuous power-law cumulant exponents and Gaussian limiting statistics with long-range violations.
AI.motivation: Defect statistics after quantum phase transitions have mostly been characterized in exactly solvable models, leaving nonintegrable long-range interacting spin chains largely unexplored despite their relevance to emergent multiscale correlations in nature.
AI.method: Time-dependent variational-principle simulations within matrix-product-state and matrix-product-operator formalisms applied to the nonintegrable fractional Ising model, complemented by analytical derivation of exact bounds on kink-number cumulants and kink-kink correlations.
AI.result: Defect-number cumulants obey power laws in driving time with exponents varying continuously with fractional order; at low order mean defect number decays slower than KZM prediction, at intermediate order KZM holds with extracted many-body critical exponents, and at large order the free-fermion limit becomes progressively accurate. Exact bounds imply a Gaussian limiting distribution, but simulations show stronger kink correlations (domain-wall confinement) and bound violations in the long-range regime; the distribution still approaches Gaussian for large defect numbers with partially broken cumulant proportionality.
AI.conclusion: Long-range fractional couplings produce continuously tunable defect-statistics exponents and quantitatively violate free-fermion bounds while preserving Gaussian limiting behavior, and the full defect statistics are measurable on existing quantum simulation platforms.

title: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications
summary: We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.

AI.tldr: Both proofs of quantumness and (quantum-verifier) oblivious state preparation are shown to coexist with easiness of nondeterministic/quantum-nondeterministic computation, via oracle separations: a classical oracle with P=NP, BQP=PSPACE, and proofs of quantumness; and a unitary oracle with BQP=QCMA and quantum-verifier oblivious state preparation.
AI.motivation: To understand whether proofs of quantumness and oblivious state preparation—generally associated with hard computational problems—necessarily require hardness of nondeterministic or quantum-nondeterministic computation. Prior work may have suggested that such primitives imply hardness; this paper tests whether that intuition holds by constructions in oracle worlds where these complexity classes collapse.
AI.method: Oracle separation constructions. (1) A classical oracle O satisfying P^O=NP^O, BQP^O=PSPACE^O, and admitting proofs of quantumness—specifically a language in IP^O ⊆ BQP^O that is average-case hard against P^O/poly. (2) A unitary oracle O with BQP^O=QCMA^O under which quantum-verifier oblivious state preparation exists.
AI.result: Existence of a classical oracle with the three stated properties, and existence of a unitary oracle satisfying the stated collapse plus existence of quantum-verifier oblivious state preparation. As corollaries: proofs of quantumness cannot yield classical or quantum cryptography via a relativizing proof; and quantum-computation/classical-communication oblivious transfer cannot yield post-quantum one-way functions via a relativizing proof.
AI.conclusion: Proofs of quantumness and oblivious state preparation do not require hardness of nondeterministic (classical) or quantum-nondeterministic computation. Their cryptographic implications are limited: relativizing reductions from these primitives to standard cryptographic objects (cryptography, post-quantum OWFs) are ruled out.

title: Simple proof of conditions requiring maximal entanglement for local state verification and discrimination
summary: For deterministic state verification by separable measurements, the Schmidt rank of an entangled resource must be at least that of the state being verified [N. Yu, R. Duan, and M. Ying, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 60, 2069 (2014)], and if the two are equal, the resource must be maximally entangled [S. Akibue, J. Miyazaki, and H. Osaka, Lett. Math. Phys. 116, 110 (2026)]. The latter was derived from a general theorem proved using algebraic geometry. In this paper, we give a simple, self-contained proof of both statements using only linear algebra. We then use these results to show that among pure entangled resources of local dimension at most $d$, a maximally entangled state of $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$ is necessary and sufficient for perfect local discrimination of a generic orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$, however weakly entangled. The same holds for local implementation of a generic orthogonal measurement.

AI.tldr: A simple linear-algebra proof shows Schmidt-rank lower bounds for deterministic state verification, and that a maximally entangled C^d⊗C^d state is necessary and sufficient for perfect local discrimination of generic orthogonal bases and local implementation of generic orthogonal measurements.
AI.motivation: Prior results (Schmidt-rank bound from Yu-Duan-Ying, and the maximally-entangled requirement at equality from Akibue-Miyazaki-Osaka) existed, but the equality case relied on an algebraic-geometry theorem. The authors want a simpler, self-contained derivation and to apply it to local discrimination/implementation tasks.
AI.method: Provide a simple, self-contained proof of both Schmidt-rank statements using only linear algebra. Then apply these results to analyze pure entangled resources of local dimension at most d for perfect local discrimination of generic orthogonal bases and local implementation of generic orthogonal measurements in C^d⊗C^d.
AI.result: The Schmidt rank of an entangled resource for deterministic state verification must be at least that of the verified state; if equal, the resource must be maximally entangled. Among pure entangled resources of local dimension ≤ d, a maximally entangled state of C^d⊗C^d is necessary and sufficient for perfect local discrimination of a generic orthogonal basis (however weakly entangled) and for local implementation of a generic orthogonal measurement.
AI.conclusion: The algebraic-geometry-based results admit elementary linear-algebra proofs, and these yield tight characterizations: maximal entanglement in C^d⊗C^d is both necessary and sufficient for perfect local discrimination of generic orthogonal bases and local implementation of generic orthogonal measurements.

title: Interpretable Quantum Photonic Generative Models
summary: We propose a physical generative model for learning correlated multivariate data based on homodyne detection of photonic continuous-variable (CV) circuits. We use an $N$-mode photonic circuit in which two-mode squeezing provides correlations, local phase shifts tune the strength and sign of these correlations, and an adjustable interferometer redistributes them across modes. We train the circuit by matching its Pearson correlation matrix to the one obtained from data. We apply affine post-processing to adjust the marginals independently while keeping the relations intact. We test the model on the multivariate distribution of standardized log returns of financial assets, showing that the photonic model can represent rich correlation structures. We reproduce empirical correlations with residuals below $10^{-4}$ for five variables and recover the correct correlation signs for $94\% \pm 1\%$ of 190 correlation pairs at twenty variables, with $86\%$ of the residuals below $0.1$. As a separate technical contribution, we develop an approach for simulating Kerr gates with small nonlinearity via a Hubbard-Stratonovich expansion, making them suitable for CV-based simulators. Our results establish CV photonic circuits as a platform for interpretable generative learning, suitable for representing and fast sampling of distributions across different application domains.

AI.tldr: A photonic continuous-variable generative model that learns multivariate correlations via homodyne detection of an N-mode squeezed circuit, matched to data Pearson correlation matrices, with a Kerr-gate simulation technique as a secondary contribution.
AI.motivation: Multivariate financial data exhibits rich correlation structures that are hard to capture and sample from efficiently. The authors aim to leverage photonic CV circuits as an interpretable, physically grounded generative platform for representing and fast-sampling such correlated distributions.
AI.method: An N-mode photonic circuit where two-mode squeezing generates correlations, local phase shifts tune their strength and sign, and an adjustable interferometer redistributes them across modes. Training matches the circuit's Pearson correlation matrix to the empirical one from data, with affine post-processing to independently adjust marginals without altering relations. Additionally, Kerr gates with small nonlinearity are simulated via a Hubbard-Stratonovich expansion.
AI.result: On standardized log returns of financial assets, the model reproduces empirical correlations with residuals below 1e-4 for five variables; at twenty variables it recovers correct correlation signs for 94% ± 1% of 190 pairs, with 86% of residuals below 0.1.
AI.conclusion: CV photonic circuits constitute an interpretable platform for generative learning, capable of representing rich correlation structures and enabling fast sampling across application domains.

title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables. Code, trained models, notebooks and the record of every IBM job: https://github.com/stein-research/reading-why
summary: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look more like the words annotators highlighted, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers on two short test pairs and kept or changed them under deletion as the model does; the evidence itself did not yet survive the device, and we work out the shots and calibration that measuring it on hardware would need.

AI.tldr: A Born-rule transformer whose every step is a measurement yields exactly computable, faithful integrated-gradient evidence with accuracy matching a softmax transformer, and compiles exactly to quantum circuits (demonstrated on IBM hardware for the readout).
AI.motivation: Language models give answers whose reasoning is only weakly estimable. The authors seek an architecture where "why" is computable exactly, via a finite, quadrature-error-free evidence decomposition, while preserving task accuracy and remaining hardware-realizable.
AI.method: They build a transformer in which each step is a Born measurement: attention as |⟨q|k⟩|^4 row-normalized, a measured product replacing the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With denominators frozen at input values, each class probability becomes a polynomial in word amplitudes, so integrated-gradient evidence is obtained by exact finite quadrature. They evaluate on e-SNLI natural language inference and compare against a same-size softmax transformer, using deletion-based faithfulness tests. The weights compile to optoelectronic optics and qubits; a coherent attention layer becomes a single circuit (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). The attention overlaps are read on IBM's ibm_kingston via Hadamard tests.
AI.result: Word contributions sum to class probability above its no-information share to 10^-11 or better (no quadrature error). With ~98k non-embedding parameters, test accuracy is 76.98±0.17% versus 76.62±0.36% for the softmax model. Deleting the top-evidence word flips the answer in 45% of test pairs (out of a 53% single-deletion ceiling), versus 32% for the softmax model explained analogously and 40% for its attention×gradient. Attention can align better with annotator highlights yet explain the answer less well: deleting its top-ranked word changes the Born Transformer's answer in only 32% of pairs. On ibm_kingston, using only attention overlaps via Hadamard tests, the device reproduced the model's answers on two short pairs and matched deletion-induced keep/change behavior; the evidence itself did not survive the device, and required shots/calibration are analyzed.
AI.conclusion: Making every step a Born measurement makes evidence exactly computable and more faithful (higher deletion-flip rate) than softmax or attention-based explanations at equal accuracy, while compiling exactly to quantum circuits; full hardware measurement of evidence remains an open engineering target.

title: Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision
summary: In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $Ω(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $Ω(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $Ω(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.

AI.tldr: This work refutes the conjectured Ω(n^(2/3)) quantum query lower bound for graph collision by giving bounded-error quantum algorithms with Õ(n^(92/139)) and refined Õ(n^(11/17)) queries, extends the technique to partial Boolean functions with positive certificate complexity 2, and proves an Ω(√(n log n)) quantum query lower bound for graph collision.
AI.motivation: Graph collision was believed to require Ω(n^(2/3)) quantum queries, matching the positive adversary/certificate-complexity barrier. The paper questions this conjecture and probes the limits of quantum query algorithms beyond the O(√n) certificate complexity barrier, aiming to separate algorithmic upper bounds from known lower-bound frameworks.
AI.method: A bounded-error quantum query algorithm is constructed to solve graph collision with Õ(n^(92/139)) queries, later refined to Õ(n^(11/17)). The approach is then generalized to all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size q, yielding an Õ((nq)^(11/17)) bound. A new quantum query lower bound is proved via adversary-type reasoning exceeding the positive adversary method's O(√n) barrier.
AI.result: Graph collision is solvable with Õ(n^(92/139)) and refined Õ(n^(11/17)) quantum queries, refuting the conjectured Ω(n^(2/3)) lower bound. The generalized bound Õ((nq)^(11/17)) applies to partial Boolean functions with positive certificate complexity ≤2 and alphabet size q, contrasting the known Ω(n^(2/3)) lower bound for large alphabet sizes. An Ω(√(n log n)) quantum query lower bound for graph collision is established, exceeding the O(√n) certificate complexity barrier of the positive adversary method.
AI.conclusion: The conjectured Ω(n^(2/3)) quantum query lower bound for graph collision is false under bounded error. The refined algorithm and generalization reveal that small positive certificate complexity does not pin down the true quantum complexity, while the new Ω(√(n log n)) lower bound shows the positive adversary method's O(√n) barrier can be surpassed, tightening the separation between upper and lower bounds.

title: Quantum Pointwise Dimension (QUPID): An algorithm for identifying classical chaos in quantum dynamics
summary: The Pointwise Dimension is a diagnostic that reveals the effective dimensionality of classical trajectories in a $2N$-dimensional phase space. The essence of this diagnostic is to find a scaling according to which density changes with radius $r$ around a point of interest in phase space. Particularly, regular trajectories are confined to an $N$-dimensional invariant torus, while chaotic trajectories explore a $(2N-1)$-dimensional energy surface. In classical mechanics, this trajectory density can be found by counting recurrences to within the sphere of radius $r$. In quantum mechanics, probability density is intrinsic, making the Pointwise Dimension compelling, but surprisingly this has not been studied in the quantum regime. In this work, we implement the Pointwise Dimension in the quantum regime using the Husimi representation of the quantum wavepacket. This implementation entails a long-time average of the time-dependent Husimi representation to obtain a stationary phase space density, and a radial spatial integration of this density over a sphere of radius $r$. The classical-quantum correspondence is excellent for both autonomous and non-autonomous systems, adding a new diagnostic to the study of quantum chaos. Finally, we explore the possibility, both classically and quantum mechanically, of obtaining the Pointwise Dimension from a time correlation function.

AI.tldr: The authors implement the Pointwise Dimension (a classical phase-space diagnostic of effective trajectory dimensionality) in the quantum regime using the time-averaged Husimi representation of a wavepacket, showing excellent classical-quantum correspondence for regular vs. chaotic motion in both autonomous and non-autonomous systems.
AI.motivation: The Pointwise Dimension reveals effective dimensionality of trajectories in 2N-dimensional phase space (regular trajectories lie on N-dimensional invariant tori; chaotic ones explore the (2N-1)-dimensional energy surface). Classically it is computed via recurrence counting, but quantum mechanically probability density is intrinsic, making the diagnostic compelling yet unexplored in the quantum regime.
AI.method: Implement the Pointwise Dimension quantum mechanically via the Husimi phase-space representation: long-time average the time-dependent Husimi density to obtain a stationary phase-space density, then perform a radial spatial integration over a sphere of radius r and extract the scaling of density with r.
AI.result: The quantum implementation reproduces classical Pointwise Dimension scaling with excellent classical-quantum correspondence, for both autonomous and non-autonomous systems; the authors also explore deriving the Pointwise Dimension from a time correlation function, classically and quantum mechanically.
AI.conclusion: The Husimi-based Pointwise Dimension provides a viable, well-corresponding quantum measure of effective trajectory dimensionality, adding a new diagnostic to quantum chaos, and may be extractable from time correlation functions.
